drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the supremum with the norm in both directions, normalizing vectors for the harder direction.
sketch_steps: setup: Let s be the supremum of ‖T x‖ over ‖x‖ ≤ 1.
derive: The bound ‖T x‖ ≤ ‖T‖‖x‖ gives s ≤ ‖T‖.
derive: Applying the definition of s to x/‖x‖ gives ‖T x‖ ≤ s‖x‖.
conclude: Thus ‖T‖ ≤ s and the two values agree.

drafts.canonical_statement: If F is a Banach space and E is a normed space, the space of bounded linear operators from E to F is complete in the operator norm.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Build the limit pointwise from completeness of F, then upgrade to operator-norm convergence.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a Cauchy sequence T_n in operator norm.
derive: For each x, (T_n x) is Cauchy in F, so define T x as its limit.
derive: Linearity passes to the limit, so T is linear.
derive: Letting m → ∞ in ‖T_n x - T_m x‖ ≤ ε‖x‖ gives ‖T_n x - T x‖ ≤ ε‖x‖.
conclude: T is bounded and T_n → T in operator norm.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Banach space, if the series of norms of a sequence converges, then the series itself converges unconditionally.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_abs_summable"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_summable"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The triangle inequality makes the sums over finite index sets a Cauchy net, and completeness gives the limit.
sketch_steps: setup: For a finite index set S, bound the norm of the sum over S by the sum of the norms.
derive: A tail of the convergent series of norms makes this bound small for every finite S beyond some N.
derive: So the sums over finite index sets form a Cauchy net.
conclude: Completeness of E gives unconditional convergence of the series.

drafts.canonical_statement: A normed space is complete if and only if for every sequence whose series of norms converges, the partial sums converge.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_abs_summable"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="partial_sums_converge"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: For the converse, extract a rapidly converging subsequence of a Cauchy sequence and sum its differences.
sketch_steps: derive: Completeness makes partial sums of an absolutely summable sequence Cauchy, hence convergent.
setup: Conversely, take a Cauchy sequence u and a subsequence with consecutive differences at most 2^{-k}.
apply_theorem: The difference series is absolutely summable, so its partial sums converge by assumption.
derive: The partial sums telescope, so the subsequence converges.
conclude: A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges, so E is complete.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite-dimensional normed space over ℝ or ℂ is complete.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Transfer completeness from the coordinate space along a bicontinuous linear isomorphism.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a basis and form the linear isomorphism with the coordinate space.
apply_theorem: Equivalence of norms makes this isomorphism continuous in both directions.
derive: A Cauchy sequence in E has Cauchy coordinates, which converge.
conclude: Applying the inverse gives a limit in E.

drafts.canonical_statement: Closed balls in a finite-dimensional normed space over ℝ or ℂ are compact; in particular the space is locally compact.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="locally_compact_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Transport the Heine-Borel theorem from the coordinate space.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix the bicontinuous linear isomorphism between E and the coordinate space.
derive: A closed ball maps to a closed bounded set.
apply_theorem: Heine-Borel makes that image compact.
conclude: Pull compactness back; closed balls are compact neighbourhoods, so E is locally compact.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every linear map from a finite-dimensional normed space to a normed space is continuous.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="linear_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bound f on a basis and compare the coordinate norm with the given norm.
sketch_steps: setup: Expand x in a basis as a sum of c_i e_i.
derive: The triangle inequality gives ‖f x‖ ≤ (max ‖f e_i‖) Σ|c_i|.
apply_theorem: Equivalence of norms gives Σ|c_i| ≤ C‖x‖.
conclude: So f is bounded and hence continuous.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite-dimensional subspace of a normed space over ℝ or ℂ is closed.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subspace_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Finite-dimensional subspaces are complete, and complete subsets of a metric space are closed.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: K is complete because it is a finite-dimensional normed space.
setup: Take a sequence in K converging to x in E.
derive: The sequence is Cauchy in K, so it has a limit in K.
conclude: By uniqueness of limits x lies in K, so K is closed.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare every norm with a fixed coordinate norm, using compactness of the unit sphere for the lower bound.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a basis and the sup norm on coordinates.
derive: The triangle inequality gives r(x) ≤ a‖x‖, so r is continuous for the sup norm.
apply_theorem: The unit sphere is compact, so r attains a positive minimum m on it.
derive: Homogeneity gives m‖x‖ ≤ r(x).
conclude: Chain the comparisons for p and q to get the constants C and D.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a proper closed subspace F of a normed space and r < 1, there is x with ‖x‖ = 1 and ‖x - y‖ ≥ r for all y in F.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pick a near-best approximation of a point outside F and normalize the difference.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume r > 0, take z outside F and set d = dist(z, F) > 0.
construct: Choose y₀ in F with ‖z - y₀‖ < d/r and let x be the normalized difference.
derive: For y in F, ‖x - y‖‖z - y₀‖ is the distance from z to a point of F, so it is at least d.
conclude: Thus ‖x - y‖ ≥ d/‖z - y₀‖ > r.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the closed unit ball of a normed space is compact, then the space is finite dimensional.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_closed_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Riesz lemma to build a separated sequence in the unit ball when the dimension is infinite.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume E is infinite dimensional.
derive: The span of finitely many vectors is a proper closed subspace.
construct: Apply the Riesz lemma inductively to get unit vectors x_n with ‖x_n - x_m‖ ≥ 1/2.
derive: This sequence has no convergent subsequence.
conclude: This contradicts compactness of the closed unit ball.

drafts.canonical_statement: Hahn-Banach theorem. A bounded linear functional f on a subspace p of a normed space E over ℝ or ℂ extends to a bounded linear functional g on E with ‖g‖ = ‖f‖.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subspace_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dual_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dual_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="restricts_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Extend one dimension at a time under a norm bound, then use Zorn's lemma; reduce the complex case to the real part.
sketch_steps: setup: Treat the real case with the sublinear bound p(x) = ‖f‖‖x‖.
construct: For x outside the domain, choose a value c compatible with the bound on the larger subspace.
apply_theorem: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal norm-bounded extension.
contradiction: A maximal extension with proper domain could be extended further.
case_split: For complex scalars, apply the real case to the real part and rebuild g.
conclude: The resulting g extends f and satisfies ‖g‖ = ‖f‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: Open mapping theorem. A surjective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces is an open map.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="surjective_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Baire category theorem to get an interior point of the closure of an image, then remove the closure by successive approximation.
sketch_steps: setup: Write F as the union of closures of T(nB), where B is the unit ball of E.
apply_theorem: The Baire category theorem gives a closure with nonempty interior.
derive: By symmetry and linearity, a ball around 0 lies in the closure of T(B).
construct: Solve T x = y by a geometric series of approximate preimages using completeness of E.
conclude: A ball around 0 lies in T(B), and translation gives openness of T.

drafts.canonical_statement: Closed graph theorem. A linear map between Banach spaces whose graph is closed in the product is continuous.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the bounded inverse theorem to the projection from the graph onto E.
sketch_steps: setup: The closed graph G is a closed subspace of the Banach space E×F, hence a Banach space.
derive: The first projection is a bounded linear bijection from G to E.
apply_theorem: The bounded inverse theorem makes x ↦ (x, f x) continuous.
conclude: Composing with the second projection shows f is continuous.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Baire category theorem to find a ball on which the family is uniformly bounded, then translate it to the origin.
sketch_steps: setup: Define closed sets A_n of points where all g_i are bounded by n.
apply_theorem: Pointwise boundedness gives E as the union of A_n, so Baire yields a ball inside some A_n.
derive: For small h, g_i h = g_i(a+h) - g_i a has norm at most 2n.
conclude: Scaling gives ‖g_i‖ ≤ 2n/r for all i.

drafts.canonical_statement: Banach-Alaoglu theorem. The closed ball of any radius about 0 in the dual of a normed space is compact in the weak-* topology.

drafts.proof_strategy: Embed the dual ball into a product of compact discs and apply Tychonoff's theorem.
sketch_steps: construct: Map f to the family of values (f(x)) in the product of discs of radius r‖x‖.
apply_theorem: Tychonoff's theorem makes the product compact.
translate: The weak-* topology on the ball coincides with the product topology.
derive: Linearity is a closed condition, so the image is closed.
conclude: The ball is homeomorphic to a closed subset of a compact space, hence compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the orthogonal complement of the kernel to produce the representing vector, then compare norms via Cauchy-Schwarz.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case f = 0 is settled by y = 0.
apply_theorem: For f ≠ 0, the projection theorem gives a unit vector z orthogonal to the closed kernel.
derive: f(x)z - f(z)x lies in the kernel, so its inner product with z vanishes.
construct: This gives f(x) = ⟨conj(f z) z, x⟩.
derive: Uniqueness follows by testing the difference of two representers on itself.
conclude: Cauchy-Schwarz and f(y) = ‖y‖² give ‖f‖ = ‖y‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: Gelfand formula. For an element a of a complex Banach algebra, the sequence ‖a^n‖^{1/n} converges to the spectral radius of a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Get the lower bound from the spectral mapping of powers and the upper bound from holomorphy of the resolvent via the power series radius.
sketch_steps: derive: λ ∈ σ(a) implies λ^n ∈ σ(a^n), so |λ| ≤ ‖a^n‖^{1/n}.
derive: Hence r(a) ≤ liminf ‖a^n‖^{1/n}.
apply_theorem: The map z ↦ (1 - z a)^{-1} is holomorphic on |z| < 1/r(a).
translate: Its power series is the sum of z^n a^n.
apply_theorem: The Cauchy-Hadamard formula gives limsup ‖a^n‖^{1/n} ≤ r(a).
conclude: Liminf and limsup agree with r(a).

drafts.proof_strategy: Openness of T is exactly continuity of its inverse.
sketch_steps: derive: The set-theoretic inverse S of T is linear.
apply_theorem: By the open mapping theorem T is an open map.
translate: For open U, the preimage of U under S equals T(U), which is open.
conclude: So S is continuous, that is, bounded.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a surjective bounded linear operator T between Banach spaces, there is C > 0 such that every y has a preimage x with T x = y and ‖x‖ ≤ C‖y‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rescale the open neighbourhood from the open mapping theorem.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The open mapping theorem gives δ > 0 with all ‖y‖ ≤ δ in the image of the unit ball.
construct: For y ≠ 0, choose z in the unit ball with T z = δ y/‖y‖.
derive: Then x = (‖y‖/δ) z satisfies T x = y and ‖x‖ ≤ (1/δ)‖y‖.
conclude: C = 1/δ works, with x = 0 for y = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: The pointwise limit of a sequence of bounded linear operators from a Banach space to a normed space is a bounded linear operator.

drafts.proof_strategy: Convergent sequences are bounded, so uniform boundedness passes a norm bound to the limit.
sketch_steps: derive: Linearity of f follows by passing to the limit.
derive: Each sequence (g_n x) converges, so it is bounded.
apply_theorem: The Banach-Steinhaus theorem gives ‖g_n‖ ≤ C for all n.
conclude: Taking limits in ‖g_n x‖ ≤ C‖x‖ gives ‖f x‖ ≤ C‖x‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero vector x of a normed space over ℝ or ℂ there is a bounded linear functional g with ‖g‖ = 1 and g(x) = ‖x‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Define the functional on the line through x and extend it by Hahn-Banach.
sketch_steps: construct: On the span of x, set f(c x) = c‖x‖.
derive: Since |f(c x)| = ‖c x‖, f has norm 1.
apply_theorem: The Hahn-Banach theorem extends f to g on E with ‖g‖ = 1.
conclude: Then g(x) = f(x) = ‖x‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: The canonical map J from a normed space E to its double dual, given by J(x)(f) = f(x), is isometric, that is ‖J(x)‖ = ‖x‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: The upper bound is immediate, and a norming functional gives the lower bound.
sketch_steps: derive: |J(x)(f)| = |f(x)| ≤ ‖f‖‖x‖ gives ‖J(x)‖ ≤ ‖x‖.
apply_theorem: For x ≠ 0, Hahn-Banach provides g with ‖g‖ = 1 and g(x) = ‖x‖.
derive: Evaluating J(x) at g gives ‖J(x)‖ ≥ ‖x‖.
conclude: Hence ‖J(x)‖ = ‖x‖ for all x.

sketch_steps: case_split: The case x = 0 is trivial.
construct: For x ≠ 0, let c = ⟨x, y⟩/‖x‖² so that y - c x is orthogonal to x.
derive: Expanding 0 ≤ ‖y - c x‖² gives |⟨x, y⟩|² ≤ ‖x‖²‖y‖².
conclude: Take square roots.

apply_theorem: The parallelogram law with the midpoint in K gives ‖v_n - v_m‖² ≤ 2‖u - v_n‖² + 2‖u - v_m‖² - 4d².
derive: Therefore (v_n) is Cauchy.
derive: Completeness and closedness give a limit v in K with ‖u - v‖ = d.
conclude: The same inequality for two minimizers shows they coincide.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the nearest point in K, show the remainder is orthogonal, and use K ∩ K⊥ = 0 for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The nearest point theorem gives y in K closest to x.
derive: Expanding the minimality inequality in directions of K shows x - y is orthogonal to K.
construct: Set z = x - y.
derive: For another decomposition, y - y' = z' - z lies in K ∩ K⊥.
conclude: A vector orthogonal to itself is 0, so the decomposition is unique.

sketch_steps: derive: Expand ‖u - v - t w‖² for w in K and scalars t.
derive: Minimality forces ⟨u - v, w⟩ = 0 by letting t be small.
apply_theorem: Conversely, orthogonality and Pythagoras give ‖u - w‖² = ‖u - v‖² + ‖v - w‖².

sketch_steps: derive: The inclusion of K in the double complement follows from the definition.
apply_theorem: Decompose x in the double complement as y + z with y in K and z in K⊥.
derive: ‖z‖² = ⟨x, z⟩ - ⟨y, z⟩ = 0.
conclude: Thus x = y lies in K.

drafts.proof_strategy: Project onto finite subfamilies and use Pythagoras to bound finite partial sums.
sketch_steps: construct: For a finite S, let y be the sum of ⟨v_i, x⟩ v_i over S.
derive: Orthonormality makes x - y orthogonal to y.
apply_theorem: Pythagoras gives ‖x‖² ≥ ‖y‖² = Σ_S |⟨v_i, x⟩|².
conclude: Nonnegative terms with bounded finite sums are summable with sum at most ‖x‖².

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Bessel's inequality makes the coefficients square summable.
construct: Completeness gives y as the sum of ⟨b_i, x⟩ b_i.
derive: x - y is orthogonal to every b_i, so completeness of the family gives x = y.
conclude: Continuity of the inner product gives ‖x‖² = Σ|⟨b_i, x⟩|².

drafts.proof_strategy: Summability follows from Bessel and Pythagoras; the limit is identified by testing against the basis.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Bessel's inequality gives square summable coefficients.
derive: Pythagoras makes the finite partial sums a Cauchy net, so they converge to some y.
derive: Continuity gives ⟨b_j, x - y⟩ = 0 for all j.
conclude: Completeness of the family gives y = x.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every Hilbert space has a complete orthonormal system, that is an orthonormal subset whose linear span is dense.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a maximal orthonormal subset by Zorn's lemma and use the projection theorem to rule out a proper closed span.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal orthonormal subset w.
setup: Let K be the closure of the span of w and suppose K is proper.
apply_theorem: The projection theorem gives a unit vector orthogonal to K.
contradiction: Adding this vector to w contradicts maximality.
conclude: Hence the span of w is dense.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Riesz representation theorem to x ↦ ⟨y, T x⟩ for each fixed y.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix y and consider the bounded functional x ↦ ⟨y, T x⟩.
apply_theorem: The Riesz representation theorem gives a unique S y.
derive: Uniqueness forces S to be linear.
derive: ‖S y‖² = ⟨y, T S y⟩ ≤ ‖y‖‖T‖‖S y‖ gives boundedness.
conclude: Uniqueness of S again follows from uniqueness of representers.

drafts.proof_strategy: Estimate ‖T* y‖² by the defining identity and use T** = T for the reverse inequality.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖T* y‖² = ⟨y, T T* y⟩ ≤ ‖y‖‖T‖‖T* y‖.
derive: Hence ‖T*‖ ≤ ‖T‖.
apply_theorem: Since T** = T, the same inequality gives ‖T‖ ≤ ‖T*‖.
conclude: The norms agree.

drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="hilbert_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="hilbert_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="operator_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="adjoint"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Combine submultiplicativity with the identity ‖T x‖² = ⟨T*T x, x⟩.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖T*T‖ ≤ ‖T*‖‖T‖ = ‖T‖².
derive: ‖T x‖² = ⟨T*T x, x⟩ ≤ ‖T*T‖‖x‖².
conclude: Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives ‖T‖² ≤ ‖T*T‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a bounded linear operator T between Hilbert spaces, the orthogonal complement of the range of T equals the kernel of T*.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="hilbert_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="hilbert_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="orthogonal_complement"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="range_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="adjoint"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite orthogonality to the range through the adjoint identity.
sketch_steps: translate: y in (ran T)⊥ means ⟨y, T x⟩ = 0 for all x.
derive: The adjoint identity turns this into ⟨T* y, x⟩ = 0 for all x.
conclude: This holds exactly when T* y = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If compact operators from a normed space to a Banach space converge in operator norm, then the limit is a compact operator.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="operator_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate the image of the unit ball by images under compact operators and use total boundedness.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε and choose n with ‖T_n - T‖ < ε.
apply_theorem: Compactness of T_n covers its image of the unit ball by finitely many ε-balls.
derive: The same centres with radius 2ε cover the image under T.
conclude: Total boundedness and completeness of F give relative compactness.

drafts.canonical_statement: The composition S∘T of bounded linear operators is compact whenever S or T is compact.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="operator_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A continuous image of a compact set is compact, and a bounded operator sends bounded sets to bounded sets.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat compact T and compact S separately.
derive: If T is compact, S maps the compact set containing T(ball) to a compact set.
derive: If S is compact, T(ball) is bounded and S sends it to a relatively compact set.
conclude: In both cases S∘T is compact.

drafts.canonical_statement: A bounded linear operator with finite-dimensional range is compact.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="range_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The image of the unit ball is inside a closed ball of the finite-dimensional range, which is compact.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖x‖ ≤ 1 gives ‖T x‖ ≤ ‖T‖, so T(ball) lies in a closed ball of the range R.
apply_theorem: Closed balls in a finite-dimensional normed space are compact.
conclude: The inclusion of R into F preserves compactness, so T is compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Absolute convergence from the geometric bound and the telescoping identity for partial sums.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖t^n‖ ≤ ‖t‖^n for n ≥ 1 makes the series absolutely convergent.
apply_theorem: Completeness gives a sum S.
derive: Partial sums satisfy (1 - t) S_n = S_n (1 - t) = 1 - t^{n+1}.
conclude: Since t^{n+1} → 0, taking limits gives (1 - t) S = S (1 - t) = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: The set of bounded linear operators from a Banach space E to a normed space F that have a bounded inverse is open in the operator norm.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="invertible_operators"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Factor a nearby operator through T₀ and apply the Neumann series.
sketch_steps: setup: Let T₀ be invertible and T satisfy ‖T - T₀‖ < 1/‖T₀⁻¹‖.
translate: Write T = T₀(I - T₀⁻¹(T₀ - T)).
apply_theorem: The Neumann series inverts I - T₀⁻¹(T₀ - T).
conclude: T is invertible, so a ball about T₀ consists of invertible operators.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a bounded linear operator T on a Banach space, λ is in the spectrum of T if and only if λI - T is not bijective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the bounded inverse theorem to identify invertibility with bijectivity.
sketch_steps: translate: λ is outside the spectrum when λI - T is invertible in the ring of bounded operators.
derive: An invertible operator is bijective.
apply_theorem: The bounded inverse theorem gives a bounded inverse for a bijective operator.
conclude: Taking the contrapositive gives the stated equivalence.

drafts.canonical_statement: The spectrum of an element of a complex Banach algebra is compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Closedness from openness of the units and boundedness from the Neumann series.
sketch_steps: derive: The resolvent set is the preimage of the open set of units under a continuous map, so σ(a) is closed.
apply_theorem: The Neumann series makes z1 - a invertible when |z| is larger than ‖a‖‖1‖.
derive: Hence σ(a) is bounded.
conclude: A closed bounded subset of ℂ is compact.

drafts.canonical_statement: The spectrum of every element of a nontrivial complex Banach algebra is nonempty.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_banach_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nonempty_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="spectrum_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Liouville's theorem to the resolvent composed with functionals.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose σ(a) is empty, so the resolvent is defined on all of ℂ.
derive: The resolvent is entire and tends to 0 at infinity.
apply_theorem: By Liouville and Hahn-Banach the resolvent vanishes identically.
conclude: An invertible element would be 0, which contradicts nontriviality of A.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a complex Banach algebra with ‖1‖ = 1, every λ in the spectrum of a satisfies |λ| ≤ ‖a‖, so the spectral radius of a is at most ‖a‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show any λ with |λ| > ‖a‖ lies in the resolvent set via the Neumann series.
sketch_steps: setup: Take |λ| > ‖a‖.
apply_theorem: The Neumann series inverts 1 - a/λ because ‖a/λ‖ < 1.
derive: Then λ1 - a is invertible, so λ is not in σ(a).
conclude: Elements of σ(a) satisfy |λ| ≤ ‖a‖, and the supremum is at most ‖a‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the constant homotopy, time reversal and time-rescaled concatenation.
sketch_steps: construct: For reflexivity take H(t,x) = f(x).
construct: For symmetry reverse time, H'(t,x) = H(1-t,x).
construct: For transitivity run H on [0,1/2] and K on [1/2,1], each at double speed.
derive: The two pieces agree at t = 1/2, so the pasting lemma gives continuity.
conclude: The three properties make homotopy an equivalence relation.

drafts.canonical_statement: A topological space Y is contractible if and only if its identity map is homotopic to a constant map on Y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the composites of the maps between Y and a one-point space with the identity.
sketch_steps: setup: Define contractible as homotopy equivalent to a one-point space.
derive: A homotopy equivalence Y to a point has a composite Y to Y that is constant and homotopic to the identity.
construct: Conversely, from id homotopic to the constant map at c, take f to the point and g sending the point to c.
derive: The composite g after f is the constant map at c, homotopic to id, and f after g is the identity of the point.
conclude: So f and g form a homotopy equivalence.

drafts.canonical_statement: If Y is contractible, then any two continuous maps from a topological space X to Y are homotopic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compose the contraction of Y with each map and connect through the constant map.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose c in Y and a homotopy from the identity of Y to the constant map at c.
derive: Precomposing with f shows f is homotopic to the constant map X to c.
derive: The same argument applies to g.
conclude: By symmetry and transitivity f and g are homotopic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write down the affine interpolation and check continuity and the endpoints.
sketch_steps: construct: Define H(t,x) = (1-t)f(x) + tg(x).
derive: H is continuous because vector addition and scalar multiplication are continuous.
conclude: H(0,x) = f(x) and H(1,x) = g(x), so H is a homotopy from f to g.

drafts.canonical_statement: Homotopy equivalence of topological spaces is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use identities, swap the inverse pair, and compose while using that homotopy respects composition.
sketch_steps: construct: The identity with itself gives reflexivity.
construct: Swapping f and its homotopy inverse g gives symmetry.
construct: For transitivity take h after f with homotopy inverse g after k.
derive: Since k after h is homotopic to the identity, g k h f is homotopic to g f, hence to the identity.
derive: The other composite is handled the same way.
conclude: So the composite is a homotopy equivalence.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonempty convex subset of a real topological vector space is contractible in the subspace topology.

drafts.proof_strategy: Contract S linearly onto a chosen point, using convexity to stay inside S.
sketch_steps: setup: Pick c in S, which is possible since S is nonempty.
construct: Define H(t,x) = (1-t)x + tc on [0,1] times S.
derive: Convexity keeps H(t,x) in S, and the vector space operations make H continuous.
conclude: H is a homotopy from the identity of S to the constant map at c.

drafts.proof_strategy: Glue the two path homotopies along the midpoint of the parameter.
sketch_steps: setup: Let F and G be the given endpoint-fixing homotopies.
construct: Define H(t,s) = F(t,2s) for s ≤ 1/2 and H(t,s) = G(t,2s-1) for s ≥ 1/2.
derive: Both formulas give y at s = 1/2, so H is continuous by the pasting lemma.
conclude: H fixes the endpoints and joins the two concatenations.

drafts.canonical_statement: For composable paths p, q, r, the concatenations (p·q)·r and p·(q·r) are path homotopic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exhibit one concatenation as a reparametrization of the other and interpolate the reparametrization.
sketch_steps: setup: Let γ = p·(q·r).
construct: Find a piecewise linear φ of [0,1] with φ(0)=0, φ(1)=1 and (p·q)·r = γ∘φ.
construct: Define H(t,s) = γ((1-t)s + tφ(s)).
derive: H is continuous, fixes the endpoints, and joins γ to γ∘φ.
conclude: Hence the two concatenations are path homotopic.

sketch_steps: derive: p·c_y and c_x·p are reparametrizations of p, so linear interpolation of parameters gives homotopies to p.
construct: For inverses define H(t,s) = p(2ts) for s ≤ 1/2 and p(t(2-2s)) for s ≥ 1/2.
derive: The two formulas agree at s = 1/2, and H fixes the endpoints at x.
derive: H joins c_x at t = 0 to p·p⁻¹ at t = 1.
conclude: Replacing p by p⁻¹ gives the last homotopy.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a path-connected space X, the fundamental groups at any two base points x and y are isomorphic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugate loops by a path joining the two base points.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a path γ from x to y by path-connectedness.
construct: Send the class of a loop α at x to the class of γ⁻¹·α·γ.
derive: The map is well defined because concatenation respects path homotopy.
derive: It is multiplicative because γ·γ⁻¹ is homotopic to the constant path.
conclude: Conjugating by γ⁻¹ gives the inverse, so the map is an isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check both identities on a representative loop.
sketch_steps: setup: Represent p by a loop α at x.
derive: f_*(p) is the class of f∘α, so g_*(f_*(p)) is the class of g∘(f∘α).
derive: Associativity of composition identifies this with (g∘f)∘α.
conclude: The identity map fixes α, hence fixes its class.

drafts.canonical_statement: A space Y is simply connected if and only if it is path-connected and every loop at any base point is path homotopic to the constant path.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce comparison of two paths to the loop formed by one path and the inverse of the other.
sketch_steps: derive: Simply connected spaces are path-connected and any two paths with the same endpoints are homotopic.
derive: Applying this to a loop and the constant path gives the forward direction.
setup: For the converse take paths p and q from x to y.
derive: The loop p·q⁻¹ is homotopic to c_x, so p ≃ p·q⁻¹·q ≃ q.
conclude: Path-connectedness and uniqueness of path classes give simple connectivity.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every contractible space is simply connected.

drafts.proof_strategy: Transfer simple connectivity from a point along a homotopy equivalence.
sketch_steps: setup: Y is homotopy equivalent to a one-point space.
derive: A homotopy equivalence induces an equivalence of fundamental groupoids.
derive: The fundamental groupoid of a point has one object and one morphism.
conclude: So Y is nonempty with exactly one path class between any two points.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a simply connected space, any two paths with the same endpoints are path homotopic and every fundamental group is trivial.

drafts.proof_strategy: Read off both claims from the uniqueness of path classes.
sketch_steps: setup: Simple connectivity means exactly one path class between any two points.
derive: Two paths from x to y lie in the same class, so they are homotopic.
conclude: Taking y = x shows the fundamental group has only one element.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let p from E to X be a covering map, γ a path in X and e a point of E with γ(0) = p(e). Then there is a unique continuous path Γ in E with p∘Γ = γ and Γ(0) = e.

drafts.proof_strategy: Subdivide the interval so each piece lies in an evenly covered set, lift step by step, and use connectedness for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: setup: Cover X by evenly covered open sets.
derive: Compactness of [0,1] gives a subdivision with each γ([t_i,t_{i+1}]) inside one such set.
construct: Inductively extend Γ using the local inverse of p on the sheet containing Γ(t_i).
derive: The resulting Γ is continuous with p∘Γ = γ and Γ(0) = e.
derive: The agreement set of two lifts is open and closed in [0,1] and contains 0.
conclude: Connectedness of [0,1] gives uniqueness.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let p from E to X be a covering map and A a preconnected space. If continuous maps g₁, g₂ from A to E satisfy p∘g₁ = p∘g₂ and agree at one point, then g₁ = g₂.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the agreement set is open and closed using sheets over an evenly covered neighborhood.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the set where g₁ and g₂ agree; it contains a.
derive: If g₁(b) = g₂(b), both maps stay in one sheet near b, where p is injective, so b is interior to S.
derive: If g₁(b) ≠ g₂(b), the values lie in different sheets, so b is interior to the complement.
conclude: S is nonempty, open and closed in a connected space, so S = A.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unpack the definition of a charted space and of a partial homeomorphism.
sketch_steps: setup: The structure assigns to each x a chart whose source contains x.
derive: A chart is a homeomorphism between open sets, so source and target are open.
conclude: The chart sends x into its target.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let f and g be maps between charted spaces, where smoothness of the transition maps is not assumed, so the spaces need not be manifolds. If f is differentiable at x and g is differentiable at f(x) in the preferred charts, then g∘f is differentiable at x and d(g∘f)_x = dg_{f(x)}∘df_x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to the chain rule in normed spaces through chart representations.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose the preferred charts at x, f(x) and g(f(x)).
translate: Differentiability means the chart representations of f and g are differentiable.
derive: The representation of g∘f is the composite of the two representations.
apply_theorem: The chain rule in normed spaces gives differentiability and the composite derivative.
conclude: The tangent map is the derivative of the representation, so the formula follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: On charted spaces, where smoothness of the transition maps is not assumed, so the spaces need not be manifolds, the tangent map in the preferred charts of the identity at x is the identity of the tangent space at x, and the tangent map of a constant map is zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute both tangent maps from their chart representations.
sketch_steps: translate: Write the maps in the preferred charts at x and at the value point.
derive: The identity map is represented near x by the identity, whose derivative is the identity.
derive: A constant map is represented by a constant, whose derivative is zero.
conclude: The tangent maps are as claimed.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a map f between real normed spaces viewed as manifolds over themselves, manifold differentiability at x is equivalent to Fréchet differentiability at x, and the tangent map equals the Fréchet derivative.

drafts.proof_strategy: The charts are identities, so the chart representation is f itself.
sketch_steps: setup: On a normed space viewed as a manifold over itself every preferred chart is the identity.
translate: The chart representation of f is f.
derive: Manifold differentiability reduces to continuity at x plus Fréchet differentiability.
derive: Fréchet differentiability already implies continuity.
conclude: The two notions and the two derivatives coincide.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build a radial cutoff from the function e^{-1/t} after passing to a Euclidean norm.
sketch_steps: setup: Transfer to a Euclidean norm using finite dimensionality and choose a closed ball in s.
construct: From e^{-1/t} build a smooth ρ that is 0 for t ≤ 0 and 1 for t ≥ 1.
construct: Define f(y) = ρ(2 - 2‖y-x‖/d).
derive: f equals 1 near x, vanishes outside the ball, and is smooth since the norm is smooth away from x.
conclude: Its support is a closed ball, which is compact in finite dimensions and lies in s.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let M be a Hausdorff σ-compact smooth manifold modelled on a finite-dimensional real space, s a closed subset and U a family of open sets covering s. Then there is a smooth partition of unity on s subordinate to U.

drafts.proof_strategy: Refine by locally finite smooth bump functions, then normalize by a telescoping product.
sketch_steps: setup: M is locally compact, σ-compact and Hausdorff, hence paracompact.
construct: Choose smooth bump functions near each point of s, supported inside some U_i.
derive: Extract a locally finite subfamily whose interiors of level sets cover s.
construct: Define f_j = g_j ∏_{k<j}(1 - g_k), which telescopes to a sum 1 on s.
derive: Local finiteness makes the sums and products smooth.
conclude: Group the functions by index i to get a partition subordinate to U.

drafts.canonical_statement: For points a, b, c of a real inner product (Euclidean affine) space, |ac|² = |ab|² + |cb|² - 2|ab||cb|cos∠abc.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the squared norm of a difference of vectors from b.
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = a - b and v = c - b, so a - c = u - v.
derive: Expanding gives |u-v|² = |u|² + |v|² - 2⟨u,v⟩.
apply_theorem: The definition of angle gives ⟨u,v⟩ = |u||v|cos∠abc.
conclude: Substituting yields the law of cosines.

drafts.canonical_statement: For vectors x, y in a real inner product space, ‖x+y‖² + ‖x-y‖² = 2(‖x‖² + ‖y‖²).

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand both squared norms by bilinearity and add them.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖x+y‖² = ‖x‖² + 2⟨x,y⟩ + ‖y‖².
derive: ‖x-y‖² = ‖x‖² - 2⟨x,y⟩ + ‖y‖².
conclude: Adding cancels the inner product terms.

drafts.canonical_statement: For points with a ≠ b and c ≠ b, |ac|² = |ab|² + |cb|² holds if and only if ∠abc = π/2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the law of cosines and use that cosine vanishes on [0,π] only at π/2.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The law of cosines gives |ac|² = |ab|² + |cb|² - 2|ab||cb|cos∠abc.
derive: Since a ≠ b and c ≠ b, the product |ab||cb| is nonzero.
translate: The equation is therefore equivalent to cos∠abc = 0.
conclude: On [0,π] this is equivalent to ∠abc = π/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: For three distinct points a, b, c of a Euclidean affine space, ∠abc + ∠bca + ∠cab = π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Draw the parallel to bc through a and use alternate angles.
sketch_steps: case_split: In the collinear case one angle is π and the others are 0.
construct: Otherwise put d = a + (b-c) and e = a + (c-b) on the parallel to bc through a.
derive: Comparing inner products gives ∠dab = ∠abc and ∠eac = ∠bca.
derive: Rays ab and ac lie on the same side of the line, so ∠dab + ∠bac + ∠cae = π.
conclude: Substituting the alternate angles gives the sum π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the power of the point and similar triangles to express everything through a, b, c, p, then close with Stewart's theorem.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The intersecting chords theorem gives |ap||cp| = |bp||dp|.
derive: Triangles apb and dpc are similar, so |cd| = (|cp|/|bp|)|ab|.
derive: Triangles bpc and apd are similar, so |da| = (|ap|/|bp|)|bc|.
translate: Substituting these and |dp| = |ap||cp|/|bp| reduces the claim to an identity in triangle abc.
apply_theorem: That identity is Stewart's theorem for the point p on side ac.
conclude: Ptolemy's equality follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: If points a, b, c, d lie on a common sphere and p lies on both the line through a, b and the line through c, d, then |ap||bp| = |cp||dp|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express each product as the absolute value of the power of p with respect to the sphere.
sketch_steps: setup: Let o and r be the center and radius of the sphere and m the midpoint of ab.
derive: Since om is orthogonal to ab, |op|² - r² = |mp|² - |ma|².
derive: For p on line ab, |ap||bp| = ||mp|² - |ma|²|.
derive: So |ap||bp| = ||op|² - r²|, and the same holds for c, d.
conclude: The two products are equal.

drafts.canonical_statement: For nonzero vectors x, y in a real inner product space, ⟨x,y⟩ = 0 if and only if the angle between x and y equals π/2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the defining formula of the angle and the injectivity of cosine on [0,π].
sketch_steps: setup: The angle θ in [0,π] satisfies ⟨x,y⟩ = ‖x‖‖y‖cos θ.
translate: Since x and y are nonzero, ⟨x,y⟩ = 0 is equivalent to cos θ = 0.
conclude: On [0,π], cos θ = 0 holds exactly at θ = π/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: A surjective isometry between real normed spaces is affine; it coincides with a bijective affine isometry.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show midpoints are preserved by a reflection argument, then upgrade midpoint preservation and continuity to affineness.
sketch_steps: setup: f is injective as an isometry, hence bijective, and f⁻¹ is an isometry.
derive: For bijective isometries g fixing x and y, g* = ρg⁻¹ρg also fixes them and moves z twice as far as g, where ρ is the reflection at the midpoint z.
derive: The supremum of ‖g(z) - z‖ is finite, so it is 0 and every such g fixes z.
apply_theorem: Applying this to ρf⁻¹ρ'f, with ρ' the reflection at the midpoint of f(x), f(y), shows f preserves midpoints.
derive: Then f - f(0) is additive, and continuity makes it real linear.
conclude: So f is a bijective affine isometry.

drafts.canonical_statement: An isometry f between Euclidean affine spaces preserves unoriented angles, that is, ∠f(a)f(b)f(c) = ∠abc for a ≠ b and c ≠ b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Recover the angle from the three side lengths by the law of cosines.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The law of cosines expresses cos∠abc through |ab|, |cb| and |ac|.
derive: The denominator is nonzero because a ≠ b and c ≠ b.
derive: f preserves the three distances, so the cosines of the two angles agree.
conclude: Cosine is injective on [0,π], so the angles are equal.

drafts.canonical_statement: The interior and the closure of a convex subset of a real normed space are convex.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take limits of convex combinations for the closure and translate a common ball for the interior.
sketch_steps: derive: For closure points, approximate by sequences in S; convex combinations converge to the combination of limits.
setup: For interior points x and y choose r with balls of radius r around both inside S.
derive: For z = (1-t)x + ty and small w, z + w = (1-t)(x+w) + t(y+w) lies in S.
conclude: So z is interior, and both sets are convex.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare partitions of [a,c] with pairs of partitions of [a,b] and [b,c].
sketch_steps: setup: L(a,c) is the supremum of polygonal sums over partitions of [a,c].
derive: Concatenating partitions of [a,b] and [b,c] gives L(a,b) + L(b,c) ≤ L(a,c).
derive: Inserting b in a partition does not decrease the sum by the triangle inequality, giving the reverse inequality.
conclude: The two-point partition gives d(f(a),f(c)) ≤ L(a,c).

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus and the norm bound for integrals.
sketch_steps: setup: γ' is continuous, hence integrable on [a,b].
apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives γ(b) - γ(a) = ∫_a^b γ'(t) dt.
derive: The norm of an integral is at most the integral of the norm when a ≤ b.
conclude: This yields the claimed bound.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonempty subset S of a group G with ab⁻¹ ∈ S for all a, b ∈ S is the underlying set of a subgroup of G.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_inv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Derive the identity, then inverses, then products from the single closure condition.
sketch_steps: setup: Pick x in S, which exists because S is nonempty.
derive: Apply the condition to (x, x) to get 1 in S.
derive: Apply it to (1, b) to get b⁻¹ in S for each b in S.
derive: Apply it to (a, b⁻¹) to get ab in S.
conclude: S satisfies the subgroup axioms.

name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the pigeonhole principle on powers of an element to produce a positive power equal to 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a in S and note that every positive power of a lies in S.
derive: Finiteness of S gives i < j with a^i = a^j.
derive: Cancel to obtain a^(j-i) = 1, so 1 lies in S.
case_split: If j-i = 1 then a = 1; otherwise a⁻¹ = a^(j-i-1) is a positive power.
conclude: S contains the identity and inverses and is closed under products.

drafts.canonical_statement: For subgroups H and K of a group, the union H ∪ K is a subgroup if and only if H ⊆ K or K ⊆ H.

drafts.proof_strategy: Argue by contradiction with witnesses a in H outside K and b in K outside H, and locate ab.
sketch_steps: translate: If one subgroup contains the other, the union equals the larger subgroup.
setup: Assume the union L is a subgroup and neither inclusion holds.
construct: Choose a in H outside K and b in K outside H.
case_split: The product ab lies in H or in K.
contradiction: In the first case b lies in H; in the second case a lies in K.

drafts.canonical_statement: For subgroups H and K of a group, the product set HK is a subgroup if and only if HK = KH.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use inversion for the forward direction and swap the middle factors for the converse.
sketch_steps: setup: Let HK be the set of products hk and KH the set of products kh.
derive: If HK is a subgroup, then inverting x in HK writes x as an element of KH.
derive: If HK is a subgroup, it contains H and K and so contains every kh.
construct: If HK = KH, define the subgroup with carrier HK.
derive: Rewrite k₁h₂ as h₃k₃ to show closure under products.
derive: Inverses of hk lie in KH = HK.
conclude: Both implications hold.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a subgroup H of a group and elements a, b, the left cosets aH and bH are equal if and only if a⁻¹b ∈ H.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_coset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_coset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_inv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Extract b as an element of aH for one direction and translate coset elements by a⁻¹b for the other.
sketch_steps: derive: If aH = bH, then b lies in aH, so a⁻¹b is in H.
setup: Conversely set c = a⁻¹b in H.
derive: Each ah equals b(c⁻¹h), which lies in bH.
derive: Each bh equals a(ch), which lies in aH.
conclude: The two cosets coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: Two left cosets aH and bH of a subgroup H are either equal or disjoint.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_coset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_coset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_coset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_coset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="emptyset"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Case split on whether a⁻¹b lies in H.
sketch_steps: case_split: Either a⁻¹b lies in H or it does not.
derive: In the first case translating by a⁻¹b identifies the two cosets.
setup: In the second case suppose ac = bd with c, d in H.
contradiction: Then a⁻¹b = cd⁻¹ lies in H.
conclude: The cosets are equal or disjoint.

drafts.canonical_statement: Lagrange's theorem: for a subgroup H of a finite group G, [G:H]·|H| = |G|, and in particular |H| divides |G|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Partition G into left cosets of equal size.
sketch_steps: translate: The left cosets of H partition G.
derive: Every coset is in bijection with H.
derive: Count elements coset by coset to get |G| = [G:H]·|H|.
conclude: Divisibility of |G| by |H| follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a finite group G, the order of every element g divides |G|, and g^|G| = 1.

sketch_steps: translate: The order of g equals the order of the cyclic subgroup generated by g.
apply_theorem: Lagrange gives that this order divides |G|.
derive: Write |G| = mq with m the order of g.
conclude: Then g^|G| = (g^m)^q = 1.

derive: So every subgroup is trivial or all of G.

conclude: A non-identity element exists since p ≥ 2, so G is cyclic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Lagrange three times and cancel |H|.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Write Lagrange for H in G, K in G and H in K.
derive: Substitute to get [G:H]|H| = [G:K][K:H]|H|.
conclude: Cancel the positive integer |H|.

derive: This is equivalent to m/d dividing k(n/d).
derive: Since m/d and n/d are coprime, it is equivalent to m/d dividing k.
conclude: Therefore the order of g^n is m/d.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show mn kills ab, then force any exponent killing ab to be divisible by m and n.
sketch_steps: setup: Let m and n be the orders of a and b.
derive: Commutativity gives (ab)^(mn) = 1.
setup: Suppose (ab)^k = 1.
derive: Raising a^k = b^(-k) to the n-th power gives a^(kn) = 1.
derive: Coprimality gives m | k, and symmetrically n | k.
conclude: Then mn | k, so the order of ab is mn.

drafts.canonical_statement: A group in which every element squares to the identity is abelian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Every element is its own inverse, so inverting a product swaps its factors.
sketch_steps: translate: g² = 1 means g⁻¹ = g for every g.
derive: ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use powers of a generator; for subgroups take the least positive exponent.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a generator g of G.
derive: Powers of g commute, so G is abelian.
construct: For a nontrivial subgroup H take the least positive d with g^d in H.
derive: Division with remainder shows H is generated by g^d.
derive: The image of g generates the quotient G/N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Construct the subgroup from a power of a generator and identify any such subgroup with the solutions of x^d = 1.
sketch_steps: construct: Take a generator g and the subgroup generated by g^(n/d).
derive: Its order is d by the formula for the order of a power.
derive: The equation x^d = 1 has at most d solutions in a cyclic group.
derive: A subgroup of order d lies in the solution set by Lagrange.
conclude: By counting, the subgroup equals the solution set, so it is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the quotient of a group by its center is cyclic, then the group is abelian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write elements as a power of a coset representative times a central element.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose g whose image generates G/Z(G).
translate: Every element has the form g^m z with z central.
derive: Products of two such elements commute.
conclude: G is abelian.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subgroup H of a group G is normal if and only if gH = Hg for every g in G.

drafts.proof_strategy: Move g across elements of H using conjugation.
sketch_steps: derive: If H is normal, gh = (ghg⁻¹)g lies in Hg.
derive: If H is normal, hg = g(g⁻¹hg) lies in gH.
setup: Conversely assume gH = Hg and take n in H.
derive: Writing gn = hg gives gng⁻¹ = h in H.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every subgroup of index 2 in a group is normal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_index"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normal_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The cosets of an index-two subgroup are forced to be H and its complement on both sides.
sketch_steps: translate: With index 2, the left cosets and the right cosets are both H and its complement.
case_split: Either g lies in H or it does not.
derive: In each case gH = Hg.
conclude: H is normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: The kernel of a group homomorphism f is a normal subgroup, and f is injective if and only if its kernel is trivial.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute f on conjugates and on quotients x⁻¹y.
sketch_steps: derive: f(gng⁻¹) = f(g)f(n)f(g)⁻¹ = 1 for n in the kernel.
derive: If f is injective, f(x) = 1 = f(1) gives x = 1.
derive: If the kernel is trivial, f(x) = f(y) gives x⁻¹y = 1.
conclude: The kernel is normal and the equivalence holds.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a group homomorphism f from G to H, the preimage of a normal subgroup of H is normal in G, and if f is surjective the image of a normal subgroup of G is normal in H.

drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugate through f, using surjectivity to lift the conjugating element.
sketch_steps: derive: For x in the preimage, f(gxg⁻¹) = f(g)f(x)f(g)⁻¹ lies in N.
setup: Assume f is surjective and write h = f(g).
derive: Then h f(m) h⁻¹ = f(gmg⁻¹) lies in f(M).
conclude: Preimages and surjective images of normal subgroups are normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: If normal subgroups H and K of a group intersect trivially, then every element of H commutes with every element of K.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show the commutator lies in both normal subgroups.
sketch_steps: setup: Let c = hkh⁻¹k⁻¹.
derive: Normality of K puts c in K.
derive: Normality of H puts c in H.
conclude: Then c = 1, so hk = kh.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a normal subgroup N of a group G, the quotient G/N is abelian if and only if the commutator subgroup [G,G] is contained in N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite commutativity in the quotient as membership of commutators in N.
sketch_steps: translate: The images of a and b commute exactly when aba⁻¹b⁻¹ lies in N.
derive: If G/N is abelian, all commutators lie in N, so N contains the subgroup they generate.
derive: If N contains [G,G], then all images commute.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

derive: Hence the commutator subgroup is contained in the kernel of f.
construct: Define φ on cosets of [G,G] by φ(x[G,G]) = f(x).
derive: Surjectivity of the projection gives uniqueness.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check that equality of cosets matches equality of values under f.
sketch_steps: translate: x ker f = y ker f is equivalent to f(x) = f(y).
construct: Define φ(x ker f) = f(x) on the quotient.
derive: The translation gives well-definedness and injectivity.
derive: φ is a homomorphism because f is.
conclude: φ maps onto the image of f, so it is an isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the first isomorphism theorem to h ↦ hN.
sketch_steps: translate: Since N is normal, HN is a subgroup containing N as a normal subgroup.
construct: Define φ from H to HN/N by φ(h) = hN.
derive: φ is surjective because hnN = hN.
derive: The kernel of φ is H ∩ N.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the result.

sketch_steps: construct: Define gN ↦ gM using N ≤ M.
derive: The map is a surjective homomorphism.
derive: Its kernel is M/N.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use image and preimage under the projection as inverse maps.
sketch_steps: construct: Send K to its preimage and L to its image.
derive: Surjectivity of π gives π(π⁻¹(K)) = K.
derive: N ≤ L makes L a union of cosets of N, so π⁻¹(π(L)) = L.
derive: Both maps preserve inclusion.
conclude: They give an order isomorphism.

drafts.canonical_statement: A group G is abelian if and only if Z(G) = G, and if and only if the commutator subgroup [G,G] is trivial.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold the definitions of center and commutator.
sketch_steps: translate: Membership of every element in Z(G) says that every two elements commute.
derive: If G is abelian, every commutator aba⁻¹b⁻¹ equals 1.
derive: If [G,G] is trivial, aba⁻¹b⁻¹ = 1 gives ab = ba.
conclude: The three conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a group action on a set, two orbits are either equal or disjoint.
