drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions 2g - |F_n - f|.
sketch_steps: derive: Passing to the limit gives |f| ≤ g a.e., so f is integrable.
construct: Set h_n = 2g - |F_n - f|, nonnegative a.e. and converging a.e. to 2g.
apply_theorem: Fatou's lemma gives ∫ 2g ≤ ∫ 2g - limsup ∫ |F_n - f|.
derive: Finiteness of ∫ 2g forces limsup ∫ |F_n - f| ≤ 0.
conclude: The triangle inequality yields ∫ F_n → ∫ f.

drafts.canonical_statement: For measurable f_n with values in [0,∞], the integral of Σ f_n equals Σ ∫ f_n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lintegral"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_seq_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_seq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply monotone convergence to the partial sums.
sketch_steps: construct: Form the increasing partial sums S_N of the series.
derive: Finite additivity gives ∫ S_N = Σ_{n≤N} ∫ f_n.
apply_theorem: Monotone convergence passes to N → ∞.
conclude: Hence the integral and the sum may be interchanged.

drafts.canonical_statement: The indicators of the intervals (n,n+1] converge pointwise to 0, yet each has Lebesgue integral 1.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pointwise_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_bump_seq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_function"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lintegral"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_bump_seq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lebesgue_measure"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Check eventual vanishing at each point and compute the integral as an interval length.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix x and pick a natural number N with N ≥ x.
derive: For n ≥ N, x is not in (n,n+1], so the indicator vanishes at x.
derive: The integral of the indicator equals the length of the interval, namely 1.
conclude: Pointwise limits may lose mass, showing the inequality in Fatou's lemma can be strict.

drafts.canonical_statement: Markov's inequality: for measurable f with values in [0,∞] and ε in [0,∞], ε·μ({x | ε ≤ f(x)}) ≤ ∫ f dμ.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_superlevel_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lintegral"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare f pointwise with ε times the indicator of its superlevel set.
sketch_steps: setup: Let E be the measurable superlevel set {ε ≤ f}.
derive: Pointwise, ε times the indicator of E is at most f.
conclude: Integrating gives ε μ(E) ≤ ∫ f dμ.

drafts.canonical_statement: If an integrable function is nonnegative almost everywhere and has integral 0, then it vanishes almost everywhere.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integrable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ae_le"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_function"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_wrt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ae_eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_function"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Markov at the levels 1/n and take a countable union.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Markov's inequality gives μ({f ≥ 1/n}) = 0 for each n.
translate: The set {f > 0} is the union of the sets {f ≥ 1/n}.
derive: A countable union of null sets is null.
conclude: Combined with nonnegativity, f = 0 almost everywhere.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is a.e. strongly measurable and |f| ≤ g almost everywhere for an integrable g, then f is integrable.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integrable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ae_le"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integrable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Check measurability directly and bound the integral of |f| by that of g.
sketch_steps: translate: Integrability means measurability plus a finite integral of |f|.
derive: Monotonicity of the integral gives ∫ |f| ≤ ∫ |g| which is finite.
conclude: Therefore f is integrable.

drafts.canonical_statement: The product measure takes the value μ(A)ν(B) on a rectangle A×B.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the slice function of the rectangle.
sketch_steps: setup: Express the product measure through the integral of slice measures.
derive: The slice of A×B at x is B if x is in A and empty otherwise.
derive: The slice function equals ν(B) times the indicator of A, so measurable rectangles have measure μ(A)ν(B).
derive: For arbitrary A and B, measurable covers of A and B give the upper bound.
derive: A measurable cover S of A×B has ν(S_x) ≥ ν(B) for x in A, which gives the lower bound.
conclude: Hence (μ×ν)(A×B) = μ(A)ν(B).

sketch_steps: setup: Let A and B be the L^p norm of f and the L^q norm of g.
case_split: If A or B is zero, then fg vanishes a.e. and both sides are consistent.
apply_theorem: For positive A, B, apply Young's inequality to f/A and g/B pointwise.
derive: Integrating gives ∫ fg/(AB) ≤ 1/p + 1/q = 1.
conclude: Multiply through by AB.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split one factor of |f+g|^p and apply Hölder with the conjugate exponent.
sketch_steps: case_split: The cases p = 1 and p = ∞ follow directly from the pointwise triangle inequality.
setup: Assume 1 < p < ∞ and that the right side is finite.
derive: Convexity of t^p shows ‖f+g‖_p is finite.
derive: Bound |f+g|^p by |f||f+g|^{p-1} + |g||f+g|^{p-1}.
apply_theorem: Apply Hölder to both terms with the conjugate exponent.
conclude: Divide by ‖f+g‖_p^{p-1}.

drafts.canonical_statement: On a finite measure space, if p ≤ q then L^q ⊂ L^p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Hölder with the constant function 1 using finiteness of the measure.
sketch_steps: case_split: If q = ∞, bound |f|^p by a constant and use μ(α) finite.
case_split: If p < q < ∞, write |f|^p as |f|^p times 1.
apply_theorem: Hölder with exponent q/p gives ∫|f|^p ≤ (∫|f|^q)^{p/q} μ(α)^{1-p/q}.
conclude: The bound is finite, so f is in L^p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, the real L^p space is complete (Riesz–Fischer theorem).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lp_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Extract a fast subsequence, sum its increments, and pass to the limit with Fatou.
sketch_steps: construct: Choose a subsequence with successive L^p distances below 2^{-k}.
derive: Minkowski and monotone convergence show the sum g of absolute increments is in L^p.
derive: Thus g is finite a.e., so the subsequence converges a.e. to a limit f.
apply_theorem: Fatou's lemma shows ‖f - f_{n_k}‖_p tends to 0.
conclude: A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.

drafts.canonical_statement: On a finite measure space, almost everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ae_fn_seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tends_in_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use continuity from above on the tails of the exceptional sets.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and define E_n as the tail union of {|f_k - g| ≥ ε}.
derive: The E_n decrease and their intersection is contained in the null set of nonconvergence.
apply_theorem: Finiteness of μ allows continuity from above.
conclude: Therefore μ({|f_n - g| ≥ ε}) tends to 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: A sequence converging in measure has a subsequence converging almost everywhere to the same limit.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tends_in_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ae_fn_seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_subseq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Pick a subsequence with summable exceptional measures and apply Borel–Cantelli.
sketch_steps: construct: Choose n_k strictly increasing with μ({|f_{n_k} - g| ≥ 2^{-k}}) ≤ 2^{-k}.
apply_theorem: Borel–Cantelli shows almost every x lies in finitely many of these sets.
derive: For such x, |f_{n_k}(x) - g(x)| < 2^{-k} for large k.
conclude: The subsequence converges to g almost everywhere.

drafts.canonical_statement: Egorov's theorem: on a finite measure space, if measurable functions converge a.e., then for every ε > 0 they converge uniformly outside a set of measure at most ε.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="uniform_tends_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="set_compl"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: For each tolerance 1/m remove a tail set of small measure and take the union.
sketch_steps: setup: Define E_{m,n} as the union over k ≥ n of {|f_k - g| ≥ 1/m}.
derive: For fixed m, the E_{m,n} decrease in n to a null set.
apply_theorem: Continuity from above gives n_m with μ(E_{m,n_m}) ≤ ε 2^{-m-1}.
construct: Let t be the union of the E_{m,n_m}.
derive: Then μ(t) ≤ ε by subadditivity.
conclude: Outside t we have |f_k - g| < 1/m for k ≥ n_m, which is uniform convergence.

drafts.canonical_statement: Radon–Nikodym theorem: for σ-finite measures μ and ν with μ ≪ ν, there is a measurable f with values in [0,∞] such that μ = f dν.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sigma_finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sigma_finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="abs_continuous"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="with_density"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Maximize the integral among subdensities and rule out a nonzero remainder with a Hahn decomposition.
sketch_steps: setup: Reduce to finite measures by σ-finiteness.
construct: Let F be the functions g ≥ 0 with ∫_A g dν ≤ μ(A) for all measurable A.
derive: F is closed under maxima, and monotone convergence gives a maximizer f of the integral.
setup: Let μ_s = μ - f dν, a nonnegative measure.
contradiction: If μ_s ≠ 0, a Hahn decomposition of μ_s - cν yields a larger element of F.
conclude: Hence μ_s = 0 and μ = f dν.

drafts.canonical_statement: Lebesgue decomposition: for σ-finite measures μ and ν, there exist a measure s mutually singular with ν and a measurable f such that μ = s + f dν.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sigma_finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sigma_finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="mutually_singular"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="with_density"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Radon–Nikodym to μ with respect to μ + ν and split along {h = 1}.
sketch_steps: setup: Reduce to finite measures by σ-finiteness.
apply_theorem: Radon–Nikodym gives μ = h d(μ+ν) with 0 ≤ h ≤ 1 a.e.
derive: The set A = {h = 1} satisfies ν(A) = 0.
construct: Let s be μ restricted to A and f = (h/(1-h)) on the complement of A.
conclude: Then s is singular with respect to ν and μ = s + f dν.

drafts.canonical_statement: Hahn decomposition: for a finite signed measure s, there is a measurable set i such that s ≥ 0 on measurable subsets of i and s ≤ 0 on measurable subsets of its complement.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="signed_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nonneg_on_subsets"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nonpos_on_subsets"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="set_compl"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Minimize over negative sets and show the complement of a minimizer is positive.
sketch_steps: setup: Call A negative if s ≤ 0 on all its measurable subsets, and let m be the infimum of s over negative sets.
construct: Take negative sets A_n with s(A_n) → m and let N be their union.
derive: N is negative and s(N) = m.
contradiction: A negative-valued subset of the complement of N would contain a negative set, which added to N beats m.
conclude: Thus i = Nᶜ is positive and iᶜ = N is negative.

drafts.canonical_statement: Jordan decomposition: every finite signed measure s is a difference s = μ - ν of two mutually singular finite measures.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="signed_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="mutually_singular"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Restrict s to the two pieces of a Hahn decomposition.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Take a Hahn decomposition with positive set i.
construct: Define μ(A) = s(A ∩ i) and ν(A) = -s(A ∩ iᶜ).
derive: Both are finite measures and s(A) = μ(A) - ν(A).
conclude: μ vanishes on iᶜ and ν on i, so they are mutually singular.

drafts.canonical_statement: Lebesgue differentiation theorem: for locally integrable f on ℝ and almost every x, the average of f over the closed ball of radius r about x tends to f(x) as r → 0+.

drafts.proof_strategy: Combine a maximal inequality with L¹ density of continuous functions.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The Vitali covering lemma gives a weak (1,1) bound for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function.
derive: For continuous functions, averages converge at every point.
construct: Approximate f in L¹ on bounded intervals by a continuous function.
derive: The maximal bound controls the set where the averages of f fail to converge.
conclude: This bad set has arbitrarily small measure, hence is null.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pass f to the quotient by its kernel and corestrict to the image.
sketch_steps: translate: Note that [x]=[y] holds exactly when f(x)=f(y).
construct: Define e([x]) = f(x), which is well defined and injective by the previous step.
derive: Linearity of e follows from linearity of f.
conclude: The values of e fill im f, so e is an isomorphism onto im f.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the first isomorphism theorem to p → (p+q)/q.
sketch_steps: construct: Consider the composite p → p+q → (p+q)/q.
derive: It is surjective because x+y with x in p and y in q has the same class as x.
derive: Its kernel is p∩q.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives p/(p∩q) ≅ (p+q)/q.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor M → M/T through M/S and compute the kernel.
sketch_steps: construct: Since S ≤ T, the projection M → M/T induces a map M/S → M/T.
derive: This induced map is surjective.
derive: Its kernel is the image T/S of T.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives (M/S)/(T/S) ≅ M/T.

drafts.proof_strategy: Define g on classes and use surjectivity of the projection for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: construct: Set g([x]) = f(x), which is well defined because S lies in ker f.
derive: Linearity of g and g∘π = f follow from the definition.
derive: If h∘π = f, then h and g agree on every class.
conclude: Hence g is unique.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix the two exact rows and the commuting vertical maps.
derive: If i3(m)=0, injectivity of i4 gives f3(m)=0, so m=f2(x).
derive: Then i2(x) lies in the image of g1, and surjectivity of i1 with injectivity of i2 shows x lies in the image of f1, so m=0.
derive: For n in the target, lift g3(n) through the bijective i4 to an element of the top row, which injectivity of i5 places in the image of f3.
derive: The difference between n and the resulting value lies in the image of g2 restricted through i2, by exactness of the lower row and surjectivity of i2.
conclude: Hence i3 is injective and surjective.

sketch_steps: setup: Assume b(x)=0 to test injectivity.
derive: Injectivity of c gives g(x)=0, so x=f(y) by exactness.
derive: Injectivity of f' and a gives y=0, hence x=0.
construct: For y in B', pick x with c(g(x))=g'(y) using surjectivity of c and g.
derive: Then y-b(x) is in ker g', so it equals f'(a(v)) for some v.
conclude: b(x+f(v))=y, so b is surjective.

sketch_steps: construct: For k in K3, choose y with f2(y)=ι3(k).
derive: g2(i2(y))=0, so i2(y)=g1(z) for a unique z.
construct: Set δ(k)=π1(z).
derive: Another choice of y changes z by an element of im i1, so δ is well defined and linear.
derive: A diagram chase gives exactness at K3.
derive: A diagram chase gives exactness at C1.
conclude: K2→K3→C1→C2 is exact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build the retraction from a section, then the direct sum decomposition, and close the cycle.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume 0→A→B→C→0 is exact.
construct: From a section s, define r by x - s(g(x)) = f(r(x)).
construct: From a retraction r, define B → A⊕C by x ↦ (r(x), g(x)).
derive: This map is bijective and is compatible with f and g.
construct: From a decomposition, compose the inclusion of C with the inverse.
conclude: The three conditions are equivalent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor a map landing in ker g through the injective map f.
sketch_steps: derive: Injectivity of f makes postcomposition by f injective.
derive: g∘f=0 makes the composite of the two postcompositions zero.
setup: Take h with g∘h=0, so h takes values in im f.
construct: Define k by h(x)=f(k(x)) using injectivity of f.
conclude: k is linear and f∘k=h.

drafts.proof_strategy: Send each basis vector to the element that indexes it.
sketch_steps: construct: Define Σa_m e_m ↦ Σa_m m.
derive: Linearity holds because the sums are finite.
conclude: e_m ↦ m shows surjectivity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Lift basis images for projectivity and use direct summands of free modules for flatness.
sketch_steps: derive: Maps out of a free module lift along surjections by lifting basis images.
translate: A projective module is a direct summand of a free module.
derive: Tensoring with a free module is a direct sum of copies of the identity, so it preserves injections.
conclude: Direct summands inherit this, so projective modules are flat.

drafts.proof_strategy: Lift on a free module that contains P as a direct summand.
sketch_steps: translate: Write P as a direct summand of a free module F via i and s.
construct: Lift the basis images of g∘s through f to get k from F to M.
construct: Set h = k∘i.
conclude: f∘h = g∘s∘i = g.

drafts.proof_strategy: Lift the identity for one direction and restrict lifts along the summand for the other.
sketch_steps: construct: If P is projective, lift the identity through the surjection from the free module on P.
setup: Conversely take i and s with s∘i = id, a surjection f and a map g.
derive: The free module is projective, so g∘s lifts to k with f∘k = g∘s.
conclude: h = k∘i lifts g.

conclude: ker(M⊗g) = im(M⊗f).

drafts.proof_strategy: Split off the free part, decompose torsion into primary parts, and split each primary part into cyclic modules.
sketch_steps: setup: Let T(M) be the torsion submodule of M.
apply_theorem: M/T(M) is finitely generated torsion free over a PID, hence free.
derive: Projectivity of the free quotient gives M ≅ T(M) ⊕ R^n.
derive: T(M) is the direct sum of its primary components.
derive: Each primary component is a direct sum of cyclic modules R/(p^e).
conclude: Combining gives M ≅ R^n ⊕ ⊕ R/(p_i^{e_i}).

derive: L_i ∩ im f stabilizes because im f is a quotient of M.

derive: If L_i ≤ L_j agree on both, then L_i = L_j, using ker g = im f.
conclude: The chain stabilizes, so N is Noetherian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Stabilize the descending chain of images and cancel the injective power.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider the descending chain im f^n.
derive: Artinian gives n with im f^n = im f^(n+1).
derive: For x, write f^n(x)=f^(n+1)(y).
conclude: Injectivity of f^n gives x=f(y).

sketch_steps: derive: ker f is 0 or M by simplicity of M.
case_split: If ker f = M then f = 0.
derive: If ker f = 0 then im f is a nonzero submodule of N.
conclude: Simplicity of N gives im f = N, so f is bijective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose a maximal submodule meeting N trivially and test it on simple submodules.
sketch_steps: construct: Zorn's lemma gives N' maximal with N ∩ N' = 0.
contradiction: A simple S outside N+N' would meet it trivially and enlarge N'.
derive: Hence every simple submodule lies in N+N'.
conclude: Since M is the sum of simple submodules, N+N' = M.

drafts.canonical_statement: A module M is semisimple if and only if M is the sum of its simple submodules.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use a complement of the sum for one direction and Zorn's lemma for the other.
sketch_steps: setup: Let L be the sum of all simple submodules.
derive: If M is semisimple and L' complements L, a simple submodule of L' lies in L, so L' = 0.
construct: Conversely, for N take N' maximal with N ∩ N' = 0.
derive: Every simple submodule lies in N+N'.
conclude: So N+N' = M and M is semisimple.

derive: Since f is mono, s∘f = id.

sketch_steps: setup: Take a, b into the pullback with q∘a = q∘b.
derive: The pullback square gives f∘p∘a = f∘p∘b.
derive: Since f is mono, p∘a = p∘b.
conclude: The universal property gives a = b.

derive: Conversely id ≅ G∘F makes F faithful and G faithful by symmetry.
derive: F∘G ≅ id gives essential surjectivity and faithfulness of G gives fullness of F.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: In an abelian category, a morphism that is both mono and epi is an isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write f as a kernel and use that f is epi to force the other map to be zero.
sketch_steps: translate: The monomorphism f is the kernel of some g.
derive: g∘f = 0 and f is epi, so g = 0.
derive: The kernel of a zero morphism is an isomorphism.
conclude: f is an isomorphism.

drafts.canonical_statement: In an abelian category, a morphism f is mono if and only if the kernel morphism of f is zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Cancel f on one side and factor through the kernel on the other.
sketch_steps: derive: If f is mono, f∘ι = f∘0 gives ι = 0.
setup: Assume ι = 0 and f∘g = 0.
derive: g factors through ι, hence g = 0.
conclude: Subtracting two morphisms shows f is mono.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix points x and a and write out the coordinates of f(x)-f(a).
derive: Each coordinate is bounded by the norm, and the norm is bounded by the sum of the coordinates.
conclude: The two bounds transfer continuity in each direction.

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute x = a + h in the definition of the Fréchet derivative.
sketch_steps: setup: Recall that the derivative is defined by a little-o condition as x tends to a.
translate: Put x = a + h, so that x tends to a exactly when h tends to 0.
conclude: The two little-o conditions coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a map f between real normed spaces is Fréchet differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="map_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="differentiable_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_map_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the increment by the operator norm of the derivative plus the little-o remainder.
sketch_steps: setup: Let L be the derivative of f at a.
derive: Write f(x)-f(a) as L(x-a) plus a little-o remainder.
derive: Boundedness of L makes L(x-a) tend to 0.
conclude: The increment tends to 0, so f is continuous at a.

drafts.canonical_statement: If real-valued functions f and g on a real normed space have derivatives L and M at a, then the product fg has derivative f(a)M + g(a)L at a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply the first-order expansions of f and g and collect the terms of order o(h).
sketch_steps: setup: Write the first-order expansions of f and g at a.
derive: Multiply them and isolate f(a)g(a) + f(a)M(h) + g(a)L(h).
derive: Bound every remaining term by a constant times the square of the norm of h or by a little-o term.
conclude: The linear part is f(a)M + g(a)L.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has derivative L at a and g has derivative M at f(a), then the composite g∘f has derivative M∘L at a.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v7"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v7"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="function_compose_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="operator_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v7"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute the expansion of f into the expansion of g and absorb the remainders using the Lipschitz bound on the increment of f.
sketch_steps: setup: Put k = f(a+h) - f(a) and expand it as L(h) plus a little-o term.
derive: Near 0 the norm of k is at most a constant times the norm of h.
apply_theorem: Expand g at f(a) and evaluate at k.
derive: Boundedness of M and the bound on k turn every remainder into o(h).
conclude: The linear part of the composite is M∘L.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a curve γ has velocity v at t and a real-valued function f has derivative L at γ(t), then s ↦ f(γ(s)) has derivative L(v) at t.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the chain rule, viewing the velocity as the linear map h ↦ hv.
sketch_steps: translate: View the velocity v as the derivative h ↦ hv of γ at t.
apply_theorem: Apply the chain rule to f∘γ.
conclude: The resulting linear map h ↦ hL(v) corresponds to the derivative L(v).

drafts.canonical_statement: A map f from a real normed space to R^m has derivative L at a if and only if for every i the component f_i has as derivative at a the i-th component of L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="map_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="euclidean_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="component_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="component_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the definition of the derivative to the remainder coordinate by coordinate.
sketch_steps: setup: Define the remainder r(h) = f(a+h) - f(a) - L(h).
translate: The i-th coordinate of r is the remainder for f_i and L_i.
derive: Finitely many coordinates are little-o exactly when the vector is little-o.
conclude: Hence the two differentiability statements are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has derivative L at a, then for every vector v the function t ↦ f(a+tv) has derivative L(v) at t=0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Evaluate the first-order expansion along the line through a in direction v.
sketch_steps: setup: Apply the definition of the derivative at the increment h = tv.
derive: Linearity gives L(tv) = tL(v), and the remainder is o(|t|).
conclude: Dividing by t and letting t tend to 0 gives L(v).

drafts.canonical_statement: If f from R^2 to R has derivative L at (a,b), then its partial derivatives at (a,b) with respect to x and y are L(1,0) and L(0,1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Compose f with the two coordinate lines through (a,b) and use the chain rule.
sketch_steps: construct: Parametrize the coordinate lines x ↦ (x,b) and y ↦ (a,y).
derive: Their velocities are (1,0) and (0,1).
apply_theorem: The chain rule along each line gives the values of L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the inner product representation and check equality at the normalized gradient.
sketch_steps: translate: Write df(a)(v) as the inner product of the gradient with v.
apply_theorem: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds it by the norm of the gradient for unit v.
construct: Assuming the gradient is nonzero, normalize it to get u.
derive: Compute the norm of u and the value df(a)(u).
conclude: The bound is attained in the gradient direction.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real-valued function on a real Hilbert space is differentiable at a and has a local maximum or minimum at a, then its gradient at a is 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Restrict to lines through a, use the one-variable criterion, then test the gradient against itself.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a vector v and define g(t) = f(a+tv).
apply_theorem: g has a local extremum at 0, so g'(0) = df(a)(v) = 0.
derive: Hence the inner product of the gradient with every v vanishes.
conclude: Taking v equal to the gradient shows that the gradient is 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has a local extremum at a and the directional derivative p in direction v exists at a, then p = 0. In particular every existing partial derivative at a vanishes.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to the one-variable extremum criterion along the line through a in direction v.
sketch_steps: construct: Define g(t) = f(a+tv).
derive: Continuity of the line implies that g has a local extremum at 0.
apply_theorem: The one-variable criterion gives g'(0) = 0.
conclude: Therefore p = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Restrict f to the segment from x to y and apply the one-variable mean value inequality.
sketch_steps: setup: The segment from x to y lies in s by convexity.
construct: Define g(t) = f(x + t(y-x)) on [0,1].
derive: The chain rule bounds the norm of g'(t) by C times the norm of y-x.
apply_theorem: The one-variable mean value inequality bounds g(1)-g(0).
conclude: Since g(1)-g(0) = f(y)-f(x), the inequality follows.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that a level set of f is open and closed in s, using the mean value inequality on small balls.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix x_0 in s and define A as the set of points of s where f equals f(x_0).
derive: Continuity makes A closed in s.
apply_theorem: The mean value inequality with C = 0 makes f constant on balls in s, so A is open.
derive: A contains x_0, so it is nonempty.
conclude: Connectedness of s gives A = s.

apply_theorem: The one-variable mean value theorem expresses each piece through a partial derivative at an intermediate point.
derive: Continuity of the partial derivatives replaces the intermediate points by p up to o(h,k).
conclude: The sum is the claimed linear map plus a little-o remainder.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the symmetric second difference through both mixed partials using the mean value theorem twice, then pass to the limit by continuity.
sketch_steps: construct: Define the second difference D(h,k) of f around (a,b).
apply_theorem: The mean value theorem in x, then in y, expresses D through one mixed partial.
apply_theorem: The same argument in the other order expresses D through the other mixed partial.
derive: Divide by hk and let h and k tend to 0.
conclude: Continuity of the second partial derivatives makes the two limits equal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express P and Q through the first derivative of f and use symmetry of the second derivative.
sketch_steps: translate: Write P(q) = df(q)(1,0) and Q(q) = df(q)(0,1).
derive: Differentiating gives dP(p)(v) = d^2f(p)(v)(1,0) and dQ(p)(w) = d^2f(p)(w)(0,1).
apply_theorem: The second derivative of a C^2 function is symmetric.
conclude: Hence P_y = Q_x.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real-valued function f on a real normed space is homogeneous of degree k, that is f(ty) = t^k f(y) for all t > 0 and all y, and f has derivative L at x, then L(x) = k f(x).

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate the identity f(tx) = t^k f(x) at t = 1 in two ways.
sketch_steps: construct: Define g(t) = f(tx) for real t.
apply_theorem: The chain rule along the ray gives g'(1) = L(x).
derive: Near t = 1 we have g(t) = t^k f(x), so g'(1) = k f(x).
conclude: Uniqueness of the derivative gives L(x) = k f(x).

drafts.proof_strategy: Solve f(x) = y as a fixed point problem and apply the contraction mapping principle near a.
sketch_steps: translate: Rewrite f(x) = y as the fixed point equation x = x - L^{-1}(f(x) - y).
derive: Since f is C^1, this map is a contraction on a small closed ball around a.
apply_theorem: The contraction mapping principle gives a unique solution for each y near f(a).
construct: Let g(y) be this solution, a local inverse of f.
derive: Inverting the linear approximation of f gives the derivative of g.
conclude: The formula for the derivative shows that g is C^1 at f(a).

drafts.canonical_statement: If g is continuous at b, f(g(y)) = y for y near b, and f has at g(b) a derivative L that is a continuous linear isomorphism, then g is differentiable at b with derivative the inverse of L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Invert the first-order expansion of f at g(b) and use continuity of g to control the remainder.
sketch_steps: setup: Put k = y - b and h = g(y) - g(b).
derive: The expansion of f gives k = L(h) + o(h).
derive: Applying the inverse of L gives h = L^{-1}(k) + o(h).
derive: Continuity of g and boundedness of the inverse give a bound of h by a constant times k.
conclude: Therefore h = L^{-1}(k) + o(k), which is differentiability with the stated derivative.

drafts.canonical_statement: (Implicit function theorem) Let E_1, E_2, F be Banach spaces, f from E_1×E_2 to F be C^1 near u, and suppose the partial derivative M of the derivative L at u in the second variable has a bounded inverse. Then there is φ with φ(u_1) = u_2 such that, for v near u, f(v) = f(u) if and only if φ(v_1) = v_2. Moreover φ is differentiable at u_1 with derivative -M^{-1} composed with the partial derivative of L in the first variable.

sketch_steps: construct: Define G(x,y) = (x, f(x,y)).
derive: The invertibility of M makes the derivative of G at u invertible.
apply_theorem: The inverse function theorem gives a local inverse of G.
construct: Define φ from the second component of this local inverse at (x, f(u)).
derive: Near u the level set of f through u is the graph of φ.
conclude: Differentiating f(x, φ(x)) = f(u) by the chain rule gives the derivative of φ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the pair of derivatives is not surjective onto R^2, obtain a linear dependence, and exclude the vanishing coefficient of φ'.
sketch_steps: construct: Consider the map x ↦ (g(x), φ(x)) and its derivative at a.
contradiction: If the derivative were surjective, an open mapping argument would contradict the local extremum on the level set.
derive: Hence there is a nonzero pair (p,q) with p g' + q φ' = 0.
case_split: If q = 0 then p is nonzero and g' = 0, against the hypothesis.
conclude: So q is nonzero and φ' = (-p/q) g'.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compactness gives boundedness, and a bounded measurable function on a set of finite measure is integrable.
sketch_steps: derive: The closed box is compact.
apply_theorem: A continuous function on a compact set is bounded.
derive: The box has finite volume, so the integral of the absolute value of f is finite.
conclude: Hence f is integrable on the box.

conclude: All three integrals agree.

drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate f locally by its derivative, deduce the measure formula, and extend from indicator functions to integrable functions.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: A linear map scales the volume of every set by the absolute value of its determinant.
setup: Partition s into small measurable pieces where f is close to its linearization.
derive: Summing gives the measure of f(A) as the integral of the absolute determinant over A.
derive: This is the integral formula for indicator functions.
conclude: Approximation by simple functions extends the formula to integrable g.

drafts.canonical_statement: The map Φ(r,θ) = (r cos θ, r sin θ) is differentiable at every point (r,θ), and the determinant of its derivative is r.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the Jacobian matrix of Φ and its determinant.
sketch_steps: derive: The partial derivatives of the components give the Jacobian matrix.
derive: Its determinant is r cos^2 θ + r sin^2 θ.
conclude: The identity cos^2 θ + sin^2 θ = 1 reduces the determinant to r.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f from R^2 to R is integrable, then its integral over the plane equals the integral over (0,∞)×(-π,π) of r f(r cos θ, r sin θ).

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the change of variables formula to polar coordinates and discard a null set.
sketch_steps: setup: Let Φ be the polar map on (0,∞)×(-π,π).
derive: Φ is injective there with Jacobian determinant r > 0.
derive: Its image is the plane minus a closed half-line, which has measure zero.
apply_theorem: The change of variables formula gives the integral of r f(Φ) over the domain.
conclude: This equals the integral of f over the plane.

drafts.canonical_statement: (Gaussian integral) For b > 0, the integral of exp(-b x^2) over the real line equals the square root of π/b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Square the integral, pass to polar coordinates, and take the positive root.
sketch_steps: setup: Let I be the integral, and note that I is positive.
apply_theorem: Fubini writes I^2 as a double integral over the plane.
apply_theorem: Polar coordinates turn it into an elementary integral of r exp(-b r^2).
derive: Evaluating gives I^2 = π/b.
conclude: Positivity of I gives the square root.

drafts.canonical_statement: The integral of exp(-(x^2+y^2)) over the plane equals π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Separate the variables and use the one-dimensional Gaussian integral.
sketch_steps: derive: Factor the integrand as exp(-x^2) exp(-y^2).
apply_theorem: The integral of a product of functions of separate variables is the product of the integrals.
apply_theorem: Each factor equals the square root of π.
conclude: The double integral equals π.

sketch_steps: derive: The integrands are continuous on the compact rectangle, so they are integrable.
apply_theorem: Fubini integrates Q_x first in x and P_y first in y.
apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem of calculus evaluates the inner integrals.
conclude: Subtracting gives the four boundary integrals with the stated signs.

apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem of calculus turns this into the difference of F_i on the two faces.
conclude: Summing over i gives the boundary expression.

drafts.proof_strategy: Existence from the least nonnegative value of a - bk; uniqueness because a multiple of b smaller than |b| in absolute value vanishes.
sketch_steps: construct: Let r = a - bq be the least nonnegative element of {a - bk}.
contradiction: If r ≥ |b| then r - |b| is a smaller nonnegative element.
setup: Suppose a = bq' + r' is another such representation.
derive: Then b(q - q') = r' - r with |r' - r| < |b|.
conclude: Hence r' = r and, since b ≠ 0, q' = q.

sketch_steps: derive: A common divisor of a and b divides r = a - bq.
derive: A common divisor of b and r divides a = bq + r.
conclude: The sets of common divisors agree, so the greatest common divisors agree.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the least positive value of ax + by and show it is the gcd.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case a = b = 0 is immediate with x = y = 0.
construct: Otherwise let d be the least positive integer of the form ax + by.
apply_theorem: Divide a and b by d; the remainders have the same form and are smaller than d.
derive: So the remainders vanish and d is a common divisor.
conclude: gcd(a, b) divides d, hence d = gcd(a, b).

drafts.canonical_statement: Integers a and b satisfy gcd(a, b) = 1 if and only if ax + by = 1 for some integers x and y.

drafts.proof_strategy: One direction is Bézout; the other uses that a common divisor divides the combination.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: If gcd(a, b) = 1, Bézout gives x and y with ax + by = 1.
derive: If ax + by = 1, every common divisor of a and b divides 1.
conclude: Hence gcd(a, b) = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For integers a, b, c the equation ax + by = c has an integer solution if and only if gcd(a, b) divides c.

drafts.proof_strategy: Necessity from divisibility of linear combinations; sufficiency by scaling a Bézout identity.
sketch_steps: derive: If ax + by = c, then gcd(a, b) divides c because it divides a and b.
setup: Conversely write c = gcd(a, b) k.
apply_theorem: Take s and t with as + bt = gcd(a, b) by Bézout.
conclude: Then x = sk, y = tk solves the equation.

drafts.canonical_statement: If integers a, b, c satisfy gcd(a, b) = 1 and a divides bc, then a divides c.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply a Bézout identity for a and b by c.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Take x and y with ax + by = 1.
derive: Multiplying by c gives c = acx + (bc)y.
conclude: a divides both summands, so a divides c.

drafts.canonical_statement: For natural numbers a and b, gcd(a, b) · lcm(a, b) = ab.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out the gcd and identify the lcm using coprimality of the cofactors.
sketch_steps: case_split: If a or b is zero, both sides are zero.
setup: Otherwise write a = da' and b = db' with d = gcd(a, b) and a', b' coprime.
derive: Coprimality shows that the least common multiple is da'b'.
conclude: Multiplying by d gives ab.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a prime p divides a product ab of natural numbers, then p divides a or p divides b.

drafts.proof_strategy: If p does not divide a then p and a are coprime, and a Bézout identity transfers the divisibility to b.
sketch_steps: case_split: Assume p does not divide a.
derive: The only positive divisors of p are 1 and p, so gcd(p, a) = 1.
apply_theorem: Take x and y with px + ay = 1.
derive: Multiplying by b gives b = pbx + (ab)y.
conclude: p divides both terms, so p divides b.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every natural number n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor.

drafts.proof_strategy: The least divisor greater than 1 must be prime.
sketch_steps: construct: Let p be the least divisor of n greater than 1.
contradiction: A proper nontrivial divisor of p would be a smaller divisor of n.
conclude: So p is a prime divisor of n.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every composite number n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor p with p² ≤ n.

sketch_steps: construct: Let p be the least divisor of n greater than 1; it is prime.
setup: Write n = pm.
derive: Since n is composite, m > 1, and so m ≥ p by minimality.
conclude: Therefore p² ≤ pm = n.

drafts.proof_strategy: A prime factor of n! + 1 cannot be at most n.
sketch_steps: construct: Let p be a prime divisor of n! + 1.
contradiction: If p ≤ n then p divides n!, hence p divides 1.
conclude: So p > n.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every positive integer is a product of primes, and this factorization is unique up to the order of the factors.

drafts.proof_strategy: Existence by strong induction via a prime factor; uniqueness by induction using Euclid's lemma to cancel a common prime.
sketch_steps: induction: Prove existence by strong induction on n.
apply_theorem: For n ≥ 2 take a prime factor p and factor n/p.
setup: For uniqueness compare two factorizations of n.
apply_theorem: By Euclid's lemma p_1 divides some q_j, and then p_1 = q_j.
induction: Cancel p_1 and apply the induction hypothesis to n/p_1.
conclude: The two multisets of primes coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a natural number k with 0 < k < p, p divides the binomial coefficient C(p, k).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use p! = k!(p-k)!C(p,k) and Euclid's lemma.
sketch_steps: setup: Write k!(p-k)! C(p, k) = p!.
derive: p divides the left side, while every factor of k! and (p-k)! is smaller than p.
apply_theorem: By Euclid's lemma p does not divide k!(p-k)!.
conclude: Hence p divides C(p, k).

conclude: Then x = u is an inverse of a modulo n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build the solution from a Bézout identity, then describe all solutions by divisibility of the difference.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Take u and v with mu + nv = 1.
construct: anv + bmu solves the system; add a multiple of mn to make it nonnegative.
translate: y solves the system exactly when m and n both divide y - x.
apply_theorem: For coprime m and n this is equivalent to mn dividing y - x.
conclude: Solutions form one residue class modulo mn.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and an integer a not divisible by p, a^(p-1) ≡ 1 modulo p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplication by a permutes the nonzero residues; compare the products of all residues.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider the residues a, 2a, ..., (p-1)a modulo p.
derive: They are nonzero and pairwise incongruent, so they permute 1, ..., p-1.
derive: Taking products gives a^(p-1) (p-1)! ≡ (p-1)! modulo p.
apply_theorem: (p-1)! is coprime to p, so it can be cancelled.
conclude: Therefore a^(p-1) ≡ 1 modulo p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and every integer a, a^p ≡ a modulo p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split on whether p divides a and multiply Fermat's little theorem by a.
sketch_steps: case_split: If p divides a, both sides are congruent to 0.
apply_theorem: Otherwise a^(p-1) ≡ 1 modulo p.
conclude: Multiply by a to get a^p ≡ a.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and integers a and b, (a + b)^p ≡ a^p + b^p modulo p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand with the binomial theorem and discard the middle terms, whose coefficients are multiples of p.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Expand (a + b)^p by the binomial theorem.
derive: For 0 < k < p the coefficient C(p, k) is divisible by p.
conclude: Only a^p and b^p survive modulo p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n and a natural number a coprime to n, a^φ(n) ≡ 1 modulo n, where φ is Euler's totient function.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplication by a permutes the reduced residues; compare the products.
sketch_steps: setup: List the reduced residues r_1, ..., r_φ(n) modulo n.
derive: Multiplication by a permutes them because gcd(a, n) = 1.
derive: Comparing products gives a^φ(n) R ≡ R modulo n, with R the product of the residues.
apply_theorem: R is coprime to n, so it can be cancelled.
conclude: Hence a^φ(n) ≡ 1 modulo n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a positive integer k, φ(p^k) = p^(k-1)(p-1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Count the multiples of p up to p^k.
sketch_steps: translate: An integer is not coprime to p^k exactly when p divides it.
derive: There are p^(k-1) multiples of p in 1, ..., p^k.
conclude: φ(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1) = p^(k-1)(p - 1).

drafts.canonical_statement: For coprime positive integers m and n, φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n).

drafts.proof_strategy: The Chinese remainder correspondence restricts to a bijection on reduced residues.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The Chinese remainder theorem pairs residues mod mn with residues mod m and mod n.
translate: x is coprime to mn exactly when it is coprime to both m and n.
derive: So the correspondence restricts to reduced residues.
conclude: Counting gives φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n, the sum of φ(d) over the positive divisors d of n equals n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Partition 1, ..., n according to the gcd with n.
sketch_steps: setup: Classify k in 1, ..., n by the value of gcd(k, n).
translate: gcd(k, n) = n/d exactly when k = (n/d)j with 1 ≤ j ≤ d and gcd(j, d) = 1.
derive: Each such class has φ(d) elements.
conclude: Summing over the divisors d of n counts all n integers once.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor x² - 1 and apply Euclid's lemma.
sketch_steps: translate: p divides x² - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1).
apply_theorem: By Euclid's lemma p divides x - 1 or x + 1.
conclude: Hence x ≡ 1 or x ≡ -1 modulo p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a natural number n ≥ 2, n is prime if and only if n divides (n-1)! + 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pair residues with their inverses for primes; a proper divisor rules out composites.
sketch_steps: setup: Let n be prime and pair each residue in 1, ..., n-1 with its inverse.
apply_theorem: Only 1 and n - 1 are self-inverse, because x² ≡ 1 forces x ≡ ±1.
derive: The pairs multiply to 1, so (n-1)! ≡ -1 modulo n.
case_split: Let n be composite with a divisor d, 1 < d < n.
contradiction: d divides (n-1)!, so if n divided (n-1)! + 1 then d would divide 1.
conclude: The divisibility holds exactly for primes.

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide k by the order and use minimality of the order on the remainder.
sketch_steps: setup: Let d be the order and write k = dq + r with 0 ≤ r < d.
derive: a^k ≡ a^r modulo n because a^d ≡ 1.
contradiction: If a^k ≡ 1 and r > 0, then r contradicts the minimality of d.
derive: If d divides k, then a^k = (a^d)^q ≡ 1.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n and a natural number a coprime to n, the multiplicative order of a modulo n divides φ(n).

drafts.proof_strategy: Combine Euler's theorem with the divisibility characterization of the order.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Euler's theorem gives a^φ(n) ≡ 1 modulo n.
conclude: The order divides every exponent with this property, so it divides φ(n).

drafts.proof_strategy: Count elements of each order, using that x^d = 1 has at most d roots modulo p and that φ sums to n over divisors.
sketch_steps: setup: Let ψ(d) be the number of residues of order d, for d dividing p - 1.
apply_theorem: x^d = 1 has at most d roots in the field Z/pZ.
derive: So ψ(d) is 0 or φ(d).
apply_theorem: The sum of φ(d) over the divisors of p - 1 is p - 1, as is the sum of ψ(d).
derive: Hence ψ(d) = φ(d) for every d.
conclude: In particular ψ(p - 1) = φ(p - 1) > 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: The forward direction is Fermat's little theorem; the converse writes a as a power of a primitive root and shows the exponent is even.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: If x² ≡ a, then a^((p-1)/2) ≡ x^(p-1) ≡ 1 by Fermat's little theorem.
construct: Conversely take a primitive root g and write a ≡ g^k.
derive: a^((p-1)/2) ≡ 1 means p - 1 divides k(p-1)/2.
derive: Hence k is even.
conclude: x = g^(k/2) satisfies x² ≡ a.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an odd prime p and an integer a, the Legendre symbol (a/p) is congruent to a^((p-1)/2) modulo p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the power is ±1 by Fermat and identify the sign using Euler's criterion.
sketch_steps: case_split: If p divides a, both sides are congruent to 0.
apply_theorem: Otherwise b = a^((p-1)/2) satisfies b² ≡ 1, so b ≡ ±1.
apply_theorem: By Euler's criterion b ≡ 1 exactly when a is a quadratic residue.
conclude: Since 1 and -1 are incongruent, b agrees with the Legendre symbol.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and integers a and b, the Legendre symbol satisfies (ab/p) = (a/p)(b/p).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the power formula modulo p and the fact that values in {0, 1, -1} are determined by their residues.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case p = 2 is checked directly.
apply_theorem: For odd p, (a/p) ≡ a^((p-1)/2) modulo p.
derive: Hence (ab/p) ≡ (a/p)(b/p) modulo p.
conclude: Both sides lie in {0, 1, -1}, which are distinct modulo p ≥ 3, so they are equal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Euler's criterion to a = -1 and read off the parity of (p-1)/2.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: By Euler's criterion solvability is equivalent to (-1)^((p-1)/2) ≡ 1 modulo p.
derive: Since 1 and -1 are incongruent modulo p, this says (p-1)/2 is even.
conclude: That is p ≡ 1 modulo 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use Gauss's lemma for a = 2 and compute the parity of the count by residue class modulo 8.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Gauss's lemma gives (2/p) = (-1)^μ with μ the number of even residues above (p-1)/2.
derive: Counting gives μ = (p-1)/2 - ⌊(p-1)/4⌋.
case_split: Check the four odd residue classes of p modulo 8.
conclude: μ is even exactly when p ≡ 1 or 7 modulo 8.

drafts.canonical_statement: For distinct odd primes p and q, (p/q)(q/p) = (-1)^(((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2)).

drafts.proof_strategy: Express both symbols as signs of lattice point counts on either side of a diagonal in a rectangle (outline).
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Eisenstein's form of Gauss's lemma gives (q/p) = (-1)^S with S the sum of ⌊kq/p⌋.
apply_theorem: Likewise (p/q) = (-1)^T with T the sum of ⌊lp/q⌋.
translate: S and T count lattice points below and above the line y = qx/p in the rectangle.
derive: No lattice point of the rectangle lies on the line, because p and q are distinct primes.
derive: Therefore S + T = ((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2).
conclude: Multiplying the two symbols gives the sign.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use that -1 is a square modulo p to show p is reducible in the Gaussian integers, then take norms.
sketch_steps: case_split: p = 2 is 1² + 1².
apply_theorem: For p ≡ 1 mod 4 there is x with x² ≡ -1 modulo p.
derive: p divides (x + i)(x - i) but neither factor.
apply_theorem: Z[i] is a Euclidean domain, so p is reducible, p = αβ with non-units.
derive: N(α)N(β) = p² forces N(α) = p.
conclude: Writing α = a + bi gives p = a² + b².

drafts.proof_strategy: Descend by q² for primes q ≡ 3 mod 4; conversely combine prime representations with the two-squares identity (outline).
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose n = x² + y² and q ≡ 3 mod 4 divides n.
apply_theorem: -1 is not a square modulo q, so q divides both x and y.
induction: Dividing by q² repeatedly shows that q has even exponent.
setup: Conversely write n as a square times a product of 2 and primes ≡ 1 mod 4.
apply_theorem: Each such prime is a sum of two squares.
conclude: The two-squares identity shows the product is also a sum of two squares.

drafts.canonical_statement: An integer of the form 4k + 3 is not the sum of the squares of two integers.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce modulo 4 and list the residues of squares.
sketch_steps: derive: Squares are congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 4.
derive: Therefore x² + y² is congruent to 0, 1 or 2 modulo 4.
conclude: It cannot equal 4k + 3.

drafts.proof_strategy: Interchange the order of summation and apply the divisor sum of the Möbius function.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The sum of μ(d) over d | n is 1 for n = 1 and 0 otherwise.
setup: Assume g(n) is the divisor sum of f.
derive: Substituting and interchanging sums gives the sum over e | n of f(e) times the sum of μ(d) over d | n/e.
derive: Only e = n survives, which gives f(n).
conclude: The converse follows by the same interchange of sums.

sketch_steps: case_split: For n = 1 the sum is μ(1) = 1.
setup: For n ≥ 2 let p_1, ..., p_r be the distinct prime factors.
derive: Nonzero terms come from products of k of the primes and equal (-1)^k.
conclude: The sum equals (1 - 1)^r = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Trivial for squares by factoring; for nonsquares use Dirichlet approximation and pigeonhole to divide two solutions of the same norm (outline).
sketch_steps: derive: If d = t², factoring (x - ty)(x + ty) = 1 forces y = 0.
apply_theorem: Otherwise Dirichlet's approximation gives infinitely many (x, y) with |x - y√d| < 1/y.
derive: For these pairs |x² - dy²| is bounded.
derive: By pigeonhole two distinct pairs have the same norm m and the same residues modulo |m|.
construct: Dividing one by the other in Z[√d] gives an integer solution of norm 1.
conclude: This solution has y ≠ 0 because the two pairs are distinct.

sketch_steps: derive: Expanding gives (x_1x_2 + dy_1y_2)² - d(x_1y_2 + x_2y_1)² = (x_1² - dy_1²)(x_2² - dy_2²).
conclude: The right side equals 1 by hypothesis.

drafts.canonical_statement: For Gaussian integers x and y with y ≠ 0 there exist Gaussian integers q and r with x = yq + r and N(r) < N(y), where N(a + bi) = a² + b².

drafts.proof_strategy: Round the complex quotient to the nearest lattice point.
sketch_steps: construct: Round the real and imaginary parts of x/y to nearest integers to get q.
derive: Then |x/y - q|² ≤ 1/2.
setup: Put r = x - yq, a Gaussian integer.
conclude: N(r) = N(y)|x/y - q|² ≤ N(y)/2 < N(y).

drafts.canonical_statement: A prime number p is a prime element of the Gaussian integers if and only if p ≡ 3 modulo 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the two-squares theorem to factor p when p is not 3 mod 4; otherwise norms and residues modulo 4 show irreducibility.
sketch_steps: case_split: Suppose p is not congruent to 3 modulo 4.
apply_theorem: Then p = a² + b², so p = (a + bi)(a - bi) with non-units.
case_split: Suppose p ≡ 3 modulo 4 and p = αβ with non-units.
derive: Norms give N(α) = p, so p is a sum of two squares.
contradiction: Squares modulo 4 exclude this.
apply_theorem: Z[i] is a Euclidean domain, so the irreducible p is prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a predicate P on natural numbers has the property that P(n) implies P(m) for some m < n, then P(n) holds for no natural number n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the well-ordering of the natural numbers to the set where P holds.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume P holds at some natural number.
construct: Take the least n_0 with P(n_0).
derive: The hypothesis yields m < n_0 with P(m).
conclude: This contradicts minimality, so P holds nowhere.

drafts.canonical_statement: For nonzero integers a and b and an integer c, a⁴ + b⁴ ≠ c².

drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize primitive Pythagorean triples twice and produce a smaller solution, contradicting minimality (outline).
sketch_steps: setup: Take a solution with least |c|; then a and b are coprime.
apply_theorem: (a², b², c) is a primitive Pythagorean triple, parametrized by m and n.
apply_theorem: (a, n, m) is also a primitive Pythagorean triple.
derive: Coprimality shows that the relevant factors are perfect squares.
construct: These squares form a new solution with smaller |c|.
contradiction: This contradicts the minimal choice, so no solution exists.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every positive integer n there is a prime p with n < p ≤ 2n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare lower and upper bounds for the central binomial coefficient, then check small n directly (outline).
sketch_steps: derive: C(2n, n) ≥ 4^n/(2n).
contradiction: Assume there is no prime in (n, 2n].
apply_theorem: By Legendre's formula all prime factors are at most 2n/3 and prime powers are at most 2n.
apply_theorem: The bound on primorials gives the product of primes up to x at most 4^x.
derive: For large n the resulting upper bound is smaller than 4^n/(2n).
case_split: Small n are checked with an explicit list of primes.
conclude: A prime exists in (n, 2n] for every positive n.

sketch_steps: setup: Assume y' = a y and put g(t) = y(t) e^{-at}.
derive: The product rule gives g'(t) = a y e^{-at} - a y e^{-at} = 0.
apply_theorem: A function with zero derivative on ℝ is constant, so g(t) = g(0) = y(0).
conclude: Multiply by e^{at} to get y(t) = y(0) e^{at}; the converse is direct differentiation.

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate H(y(t)) - G(t) by the chain rule and check that the derivative vanishes.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The chain rule gives (H∘y)'(t) = (1/h(y(t))) g(t) h(y(t)).
derive: Since h(y(t)) ≠ 0 this equals g(t), so (H∘y - G)' = 0.
apply_theorem: A function with zero derivative on ℝ is constant.
conclude: Hence H(y(t)) - G(t) = H(y(s)) - G(s).

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate the reciprocal of the denominator and compare with r y (1 - y) after clearing denominators.
sketch_steps: setup: Put D(s) = 1 + C e^{-rs}, so D'(t) = -r C e^{-rt} and D(t) ≠ 0.
apply_theorem: The quotient rule gives y'(t) = r C e^{-rt} / D(t)^2.
derive: Since D - 1 = C e^{-rt}, we have r y (1 - y) = r C e^{-rt} / D(t)^2.
conclude: The two expressions agree.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that f e^{-au} is nonincreasing using the sign of its derivative.
sketch_steps: setup: Put g(u) = f(u) e^{-au} on [s,t].
derive: On (s,t) we have g'(u) = (f'(u) - a f(u)) e^{-au} ≤ 0.
apply_theorem: A continuous function with nonpositive derivative on the interior is nonincreasing.
conclude: g(t) ≤ g(s), and multiplying by e^{at} > 0 gives the bound.

sketch_steps: setup: Extend u continuously from [a,b] to ℝ so that the integral is differentiable everywhere.
translate: Put v(t) = c + K ∫_a^t u, so u ≤ v and v' = K u on [a,b].
derive: Since K ≥ 0, v' = K u ≤ K v, so (v e^{-K(t-a)})' ≤ 0.
apply_theorem: A function with nonpositive derivative is nonincreasing, so v(t) e^{-K(t-a)} ≤ v(a) = c.
conclude: Therefore u(t) ≤ v(t) ≤ c e^{K(t-a)}.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the norm with the exact solution of φ' = Kφ + ε, φ(a) = δ, using a slope comparison on the right.
sketch_steps: translate: The upper right slope of ‖f‖ is at most ‖f'‖, hence at most K‖f‖ + ε.
construct: The bound φ(x) = δ e^{K(x-a)} + (ε/K)(e^{K(x-a)} - 1) satisfies φ' = Kφ + ε and φ(a) = δ.
contradiction: With ε slightly increased, ‖f‖ cannot cross φ, since at a first crossing the slopes would contradict.
conclude: Letting the increase tend to 0 gives the bound for ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: (Picard–Lindelöf) Let E be a real Banach space, t₀ ∈ [tmin, tmax], and suppose that on the closed ball B(x₀, a) the field f(t, x) is K-Lipschitz in x, continuous in t and bounded in norm by L, with L·max(tmax - t₀, t₀ - tmin) ≤ a. Then x' = f(t, x), x(t₀) = x₀ has a solution on [tmin, tmax].

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the initial value problem as a fixed-point equation for the Picard operator and use a contraction argument for an iterate.
sketch_steps: translate: A solution is the same as a fixed point of Φ(α)(t) = x₀ + ∫_{t₀}^t f(s, α(s)) ds.
setup: Let X be the complete space of continuous curves with values in the closed ball B(x₀, a).
derive: The bound L and the time-width condition show that Φ maps X into X.
derive: The Lipschitz condition gives ‖Φ^n α - Φ^n β‖ ≤ (K T)^n / n! ‖α - β‖, so an iterate is a contraction.
apply_theorem: Banach's fixed point theorem gives a fixed point of Φ.
conclude: Differentiating the integral equation gives the solution.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exhibit the zero function and t|t| and verify the equation for t|t| separately for t < 0, t = 0, t > 0.
sketch_steps: construct: Take y₁ ≡ 0 and y₂(t) = t|t|.
case_split: For t > 0 y₂ agrees with t² near t, for t < 0 with -t² near t.
derive: At t = 0 both one-sided derivatives vanish, so y₂'(t) = 2|t| everywhere.
derive: Since √|t|t|| = |t|, the equation y₂' = 2√|y₂| holds.
conclude: y₂(1) = 1 ≠ 0 = y₁(1), so uniqueness fails.

drafts.canonical_statement: If r is a root of r² + a r + b = 0, then y(t) = e^{rt} satisfies y'' + a y' + b y = 0, with y' = r e^{rt}.
